concepts.statement: The conversion efficiency is the ratio of what we get to what we spend: for a heat engine, the net work output divided by the heat transfer into the engine. Since the work is the difference of the two heat transfers, the efficiency is also one minus the ratio of the heat transfer to the cold reservoir to the heat transfer from the hot one, which shows that an efficiency of one would need no heat transfer to the environment at all. All the Q's are positive, with direction shown by sign or on the schematic.

forms.condition: cyclical process

concepts.name: Finding an engine’s efficiency
concepts.statement: Given any two of the heat transfer into an engine, the heat transfer to the environment and the work output, the cycle's energy balance gives the third, and the efficiency follows as work over heat in. Run the other way, a stated efficiency and a heat input give the work and the waste heat. A large power station is a heat engine, so the same arithmetic gives its daily output, its efficiency and, with the fuel's energy content, the fuel it burns and the carbon dioxide it releases.

concepts.name: Otto cycle
concepts.statement: The Otto cycle is the thermodynamic cycle of the four-stroke gasoline engine, two adiabatic processes and two isochoric ones. An adiabatic compression corresponds to the compression stroke, heat transfer in at constant volume to the burning of the fuel, an adiabatic expansion to the power stroke, and heat transfer out at constant volume to the exhaust and intake. The work out along the expansion exceeds the work in along the compression because the pressure is higher, so there is a net work output, and the cooler the compression and the hotter the expansion the larger the loop and the more efficient the engine, which points to the reservoir temperatures as what sets the limit.

concepts.name: Second law of thermodynamics
concepts.statement: The second law of thermodynamics states that heat transfer occurs spontaneously only from a hotter body to a colder one, never the reverse, and that no cyclical process can convert heat transfer from a reservoir completely into work. The chapter gives it in several equivalent forms.

concepts.name: Carnot cycle
concepts.statement: Sadi Carnot devised in 1824 a theoretical cycle that is the most efficient cyclical process possible, made of two isothermal and two adiabatic processes, all of them reversible. Any heat engine that uses it is a Carnot engine. What defines the cycle is that only reversible processes are used, since irreversible processes involve dissipative factors such as friction and turbulence that increase the heat transfer to the environment and lower the efficiency. The ideal Carnot engine has zero power, like the drinking bird, which is why it is a limit and not a design.

concepts.name: Third expression of the second law
concepts.statement: Stated in terms of reversible processes, the second law has a third form: a Carnot engine operating between two given temperatures has the greatest possible efficiency of any heat engine operating between them, and all engines employing only reversible processes have this same maximum efficiency between the same temperatures. What Carnot discovered in his study of steam engines was this law.

concepts.name: Carnot efficiency
concepts.statement: For a perfect heat engine the ratio of the heat transfer to the cold reservoir to the heat transfer from the hot one equals the ratio of the absolute temperatures of the two reservoirs, so the maximum efficiency is one minus the cold temperature over the hot, both in kelvins. An efficiency of 100% would need a cold reservoir at absolute zero, which is impossible in practice and in theory, and the greatest efficiencies come from the hottest possible hot reservoir and the coldest possible cold one. No real engine reaches the Carnot efficiency.

forms.condition: temperatures in kelvins or any other absolute scale
Carnot engine, temperatures in kelvins
any reversible process

concepts.name: Finding a Carnot efficiency
concepts.statement: Convert the reservoir temperatures to kelvins and the Carnot efficiency follows; or use a stated efficiency and one reservoir temperature to find the other. A real engine that reaches some fraction of the maximum works the same way. Two engines in series, the second running on the exhaust of the first, have an overall Carnot efficiency equal to that of one engine between the outer temperatures.

concepts.name: Real engines and the Carnot efficiency
concepts.statement: All real processes are irreversible, so no real engine is as efficient as a Carnot engine between the same reservoirs; a nuclear station's 35% is a little better than 0.7 of its maximum, and coal, oil and gas stations reach about 42% because their boilers run hotter. Even the best engine has dissipative processes in its peripheral equipment, such as transformers and transmissions, which convert some of the work output back into heat transfer to the environment and lower the overall efficiency further.

concepts.name: Carnot engine
concepts.statement: A Carnot engine is a heat engine that runs on the Carnot cycle, using only reversible processes.

concepts.name: Heat pump
concepts.statement: Heat pumps, air conditioners and refrigerators move heat from cold to hot. They are heat engines run backward: heat flows out of a cold reservoir and into a hot one, and this requires a work input, which itself becomes heat transfer. The heat transfer to the hot reservoir is the heat from the cold reservoir plus the work. A heat pump's mission is the heat delivered to a warm space; a refrigerator's or an air conditioner's is the heat removed from a cold one. You pay only for the work and get the heat from the cold outdoors at no cost.

forms.condition: heat pump, refrigerator or air conditioner; all three quantities positive

concepts.name: Components of a heat pump
concepts.statement: A heat pump has a condenser, an expansion valve, an evaporator and a compressor, joined in a loop that a working fluid runs round. In the outdoor evaporator the fluid takes heat from the cold air and becomes a gas; the electrically driven compressor raises its temperature and pressure and forces it into the indoor condenser coils, where, being hotter than the room, it gives up heat and condenses; the liquid then passes back through the expansion valve and cools as it expands. In a cooling cycle the two coils exchange roles and the fluid runs the other way.

concepts.name: Coefficient of performance of a heat pump
concepts.statement: A heat pump earns its keep by the heat it delivers to the warm space compared with the work it takes, so its coefficient of performance is the heat transfer to the hot reservoir divided by the work input. A heat engine's efficiency is the work over that same heat transfer, so the coefficient of performance is the reciprocal of the efficiency. Because every efficiency is less than one, the coefficient is always greater than one: a heat pump always delivers more heat than the work put into it.

concepts.name: Heat pumps and temperature difference
concepts.statement: Because the coefficient of performance is the reciprocal of the efficiency and the Carnot efficiency shrinks as the two reservoir temperatures approach one another, a heat pump does best when the difference between outdoors and indoors is small and worst in very cold climates. Friction and other irreversible processes do not help a heat pump as they lower an engine's efficiency; they take part of the work input as heat before it reaches the pump and lower the coefficient of performance. Real heat pumps reach values from about 2 to 4, and they are most economical where winters are mild and summers warm.

concepts.name: Coefficient of performance of a refrigerator
concepts.statement: An air conditioner or refrigerator earns its keep by the heat it removes from the cold environment compared with the work input, so its coefficient of performance is the heat transfer from the cold reservoir divided by the work. What a heat pump counts as its benefit, a refrigerator counts as waste heat. The heat to the hot reservoir is the heat from the cold one plus the work, so for the same engine between the same temperatures the refrigerator's coefficient is the heat pump's minus one. Real refrigerators reach values from 2 to 6 because their temperature differences are small.

forms.condition: the same heat engine used as an air conditioner or a heat pump between the same two temperatures

concepts.name: Finding the best coefficient of performance
concepts.statement: A Carnot engine reversed gives the best possible heat pump or refrigerator, so the best coefficient of performance follows from the Carnot efficiency between the two reservoir temperatures in kelvins: the reciprocal for a heat pump, and one less than that for a refrigerator. With a work input given, the heat delivered or removed follows, and with a price per kilowatt-hour so does the cost, which is how the section compares a heat pump with burning natural gas.

concepts.name: Energy efficiency rating
concepts.statement: The energy efficiency rating is a coefficient of performance in mixed units: British thermal units of heat transfer from the cold environment per hour, divided by watts of power input. Several countries still use it for room air conditioners, which carry ratings from 6 to 12. The rating is not the same as the coefficient of performance, but it serves for comparison: the greater the rating, the cheaper the unit is to run and the more it is likely to cost to buy.

forms.condition: Q_c in British thermal units, t_1 in hours, W in joules, t_2 in seconds

concepts.name: Solving thermodynamics problems
concepts.statement: Work a thermodynamics problem in seven steps. Decide whether heat, work or internal energy is involved. Identify the system and draw a labeled diagram of the energy flow. List the unknowns, remembering that a maximum efficiency means a Carnot engine and that efficiency is not the same as coefficient of performance. List the knowns, distinguishing heat in from heat out and work in from work out, and name the kind of process. Solve the appropriate equation, substitute with units, and check that the answer is reasonable: an efficiency below one and a coefficient of performance above one.

concepts.name: Entropy
concepts.statement: Entropy is a measure of a system's disorder and of the unavailability of its energy to do work. All forms of energy can do work, but it is not always possible, even in principle, to convert all of a system's energy into work, and entropy measures how much cannot be converted. Like internal energy it is a property of state: the entropy of a system depends only on its state and not on how it got there, so you can compute its change for any process, real or imagined.

concepts.name: Change in entropy
concepts.statement: The change in entropy of a system in a reversible process is the heat transfer, positive into the system and negative out of it, divided by the absolute temperature at which it takes place, in joules per kelvin. For a Carnot cycle the heat transfers at the two reservoirs are in the ratio of their absolute temperatures, so this ratio is the same at both. Where the temperature changes a little during the process, use the average temperature. The definition holds strictly for reversible processes, but because entropy is a property of state, you can find the change for any real process by imagining a reversible one between the same two states.

forms.condition: reversible process, or any process whose end states a reversible process could join

concepts.name: Entropy increase in irreversible processes
concepts.statement: Spontaneous heat transfer from hot to cold is irreversible, and its total entropy change is found by imagining a reversible loss from the hot reservoir and a reversible gain by the cold one. Because the change in entropy is the heat over the temperature, the same heat makes a larger change at the lower temperature: the hot reservoir's loss is smaller than the cold reservoir's gain, and the total increases. The result is general: every irreversible process increases the entropy of the system.

concepts.name: Second law in terms of entropy
terms: second law of thermodynamics stated in terms of entropy
concepts.statement: The total change in entropy over a Carnot cycle is the hot reservoir's loss plus the cold reservoir's gain, and because the two heat transfers are in the ratio of the temperatures the total is zero; this holds for any reversible process, which changes neither the entropy of the system nor that of its surroundings. Real processes are irreversible and increase the total entropy. So there are only two possibilities, and the fourth form of the second law says so: entropy is constant in a reversible process and increases in an irreversible one, and it never decreases. Heat cannot flow spontaneously from cold to hot because entropy would decrease. Entropy, unlike energy, is not conserved.

forms.condition: Carnot engine, and any reversible process

concepts.name: Unavailable energy
concepts.statement: When entropy increases, a certain amount of energy becomes permanently unavailable to do work. The energy is not lost, but its character changes, so some of it can never again become an organized force acting through a distance. The amount that becomes unavailable is the increase in entropy times the lowest temperature used. Two perfect engines fed the same heat give different work when one receives it only after the heat has fallen to a colder reservoir, and the difference is exactly this quantity.

concepts.name: Heat death of the universe
concepts.statement: As entropy increases, less and less of the energy in the universe is available to do work. Temperature differences, which heat engines run on, arose as the universe matured and are being used up. On Earth the stores of fuel and the temperature differences behind wind, geothermal and tidal energy will be spent. The Sun will replenish some of them for another five billion years, but in the very long run all stars will die and all temperatures will equalize. The universe is headed for thermodynamic equilibrium, maximum entropy, when no work can be done, though calculations suggest that is at least 10¹⁰⁰ years away.

concepts.name: Entropy and disorder
concepts.statement: Entropy is related not only to the unavailability of energy but also to disorder, as Boltzmann first proposed. Melting a block of ice turns a structured arrangement of molecules into a liquid with no fixed positions, and the entropy rises by a large amount. Mixing equal masses of warm and cool water has three results at once. The entropy increases; some energy becomes unavailable to do work, because no temperature difference remains to run an engine; and a single mass at one temperature is less orderly than two masses at two. These three results are essentially equivalent.

concepts.name: Local decreases in entropy
concepts.statement: Living organisms are highly structured and much lower in entropy than what they grow from, and some take this to mean that evolution violates the second law. It does not. The entropy of one part of the universe can always decrease, provided the environment's entropy increases by more, so that the total change is positive. Picking up scattered marbles or building a bridge lowers the entropy of those systems by energy transfer. The Earth, intercepting a small part of the Sun's heat transfer into deep space, is a heat engine of high complexity that produces small local decreases in entropy at the cost of a large total increase.

forms.condition: any real process

concepts.name: Finding an entropy change
concepts.statement: The heat transfer and the absolute temperature at which it takes place give the change in entropy. Where the temperature changes a little, use the average temperature in kelvins, and for a phase change the heat transfer is the mass times the latent heat. For a transfer between two bodies, the total change is the sum of a negative change at the hotter temperature and a positive one at the colder. Multiply the total by the lowest temperature to find the energy made unavailable.

concepts.name: Macrostate and microstate
concepts.statement: A macrostate is an overall property of a system, such as the total number of heads and tails in a toss or the pressure, volume and temperature of a gas; it does not specify the details. A microstate is a detailed description of every element of the system, such as the order in which the heads and tails came up or the positions and velocities of every atom. Each macrostate can be reached by some number of microstates, and the analysis assumes that every microstate is equally probable, which requires the coins to be fair.

concepts.name: Probability of disorder
concepts.statement: The most orderly macrostates, all heads or all tails, have the fewest microstates and are the least likely; the most disorderly, an even split, have the most and are the most likely. With five coins the odds are 30 to 2 that a toss leaves an orderly array less orderly; with a hundred, there is one way to get all heads and 10²⁹ ways to get fifty, and a toss a second would produce all heads once in 2 × 10²² years, a trillion times the age of the universe. The growth in the odds favoring disorder continues as the system grows, so for the atoms of a gas the orderly macrostate, all in one corner, is so unlikely that it never happens.

concepts.name: Boltzmann’s entropy
concepts.statement: Boltzmann proved that the entropy of a system in a given macrostate is Boltzmann's constant times the natural logarithm of the number of microstates corresponding to that macrostate, and that this expression agrees with the definition of the change in entropy as heat transfer over temperature. Because the number of microstates is proportional to the probability of the macrostate, entropy is directly related to probability: the more likely the state, the greater its entropy. This explains the second law at the most basic level. A decrease in entropy is a move to a less probable state, and for a macroscopic system the odds against it are so long that no one ever observes it.

forms.condition: k the Boltzmann constant, W the number of microstates of the macrostate

concepts.name: Finding entropy from microstates
concepts.statement: The change in entropy between two macrostates is Boltzmann's constant times the difference of the logarithms of their numbers of microstates, read from a table or counted. The ratio of the two numbers of microstates tells how much more likely one macrostate is than the other, and so whether a given decrease in entropy could ever occur. A change of 10⁻²¹ J/K is a one in 10³⁰ chance, so a macroscopic decrease of the order of 10³ J/K is an utter impossibility.

forms.latex: \Delta S = S_{\text{f}} - S_{\text{i}} = k\ln W_{\text{f}} - k\ln W_{\text{i}}

concepts.name: Statistical interpretation of the second law
concepts.statement: The several statements of the second law say what happens; the statistical view says why. Heat flows only from hot to cold, energy becomes ever less available and the universe grows more disorderly because disorder is vastly more probable than order, and a macroscopic system has so many atoms that the improbable never occurs. The gas that fills its container will never gather in one corner. Energy transfer from outside could force it there and lower its entropy, but only at the cost of a larger increase elsewhere, and left alone it disperses again. Entropy can decrease, but for any macroscopic system the outcome is so unlikely that no one will ever observe it.

concepts.name: Solving entropy problems
concepts.statement: Work an entropy problem in seven steps. Decide whether entropy is involved. Identify the system and draw a labeled diagram of the energy flow. List the unknowns. List the knowns, identifying the heat transfer, the temperature at which it takes place and the initial and final states. Solve the appropriate equation, remembering that a reversible process joining any two states gives the change in entropy between them. Substitute with units, and check that the answer is reasonable: the total entropy increases in any real process, and disordered states are the more probable.

concepts.name: Macrostate
concepts.statement: A macrostate is an overall property of a system, such as the total number of heads and tails in a set of coin tosses, without regard to the order in which they arise.

concepts.name: Microstate
concepts.statement: A microstate is one detailed arrangement of a system, such as one particular sequence of heads and tails, and many microstates may belong to the same macrostate.

concepts.name: Statistical analysis
concepts.statement: Statistical analysis examines a system by counting its possibilities, such as the microstates that belong to each macrostate, to find how likely each outcome is.

concepts.name: 热量
concepts.statement: 热量是由温度差引起的能量自发传递。当两个温度不同的物体相接触时，能量由较热的物体传向较冷的物体，直到它们达到相同的温度；在此过程中没有力作用一段距离，所以这种传递不是功。因此，热量是一种传递中的能量形式：它只在温度差驱动它的时候存在，一旦温度相等便终止。

concepts.name: 热量与温度之别
concepts.statement: 我们可能会说热量令人难以忍受，而实际想说的是温度很高。热量是能量的一种形式，以焦耳计量；温度不是能量，而是原子和分子平均动能的量度。之所以产生这种混淆，是因为我们感觉到的是热量的流动，而不是温度本身。把两者区分开，本章后面的内容才能说明，加入热量并不一定会使温度升高。

concepts.name: 热量的单位
concepts.statement: 由于热量是能量的一种形式，其 SI 单位是焦耳，但热量也用卡来计量，卡是使 1.00 g 水的温度升高 1.00 °C 所需的能量，而最常用的是千卡，它使 1.00 kg 水升高同样的温度。食物大卡就是千卡，这一点很难从包装标签上确定，而在这些单位之间换算是本章几乎每道题的一部分。

concepts.name: 热功当量
concepts.statement: 做功也可以改变物质的温度，詹姆斯·普雷斯科特·焦耳的实验确立了热功当量，即产生与热传递相同效果的功。现代最佳值是 1.000 kcal = 4186 J，我们把它当作两个能量单位之间的换算关系。在焦耳的装置中，下落的重物带动水中的桨叶转动。重力势能变为动能，黏度把它随机化为分子的运动，温度计的示数恰好像加入热量时一样上升。

forms.condition: 15 °C 卡

concepts.name: 由热量或功改变内能
concepts.statement: 加给系统的热量会改变其内能，通常也改变其温度，对系统做功（通过搅拌或摩擦）同样如此。系统有确定的内能，却没有热含量，也没有功含量：能量一旦进入内部，样品本身就看不出它是以哪种方式进来的。这就是本书说热传递而不说热量的原因，也是第 15 章建立热力学第一定律所依据的思想。

concepts.name: 千卡
concepts.statement: 千卡是热量的单位，等于 1000 卡，即使 1.00 kg 水的温度升高 1.00 °C 所需的能量。食物大卡就是千卡。

concepts.name: 热传递中的因素
concepts.statement: 实验表明，使物体温度改变所传递的热量取决于三个因素：温度的变化、物体的质量，以及物质及其相。给定质量的温度变化加倍，所需热量加倍；质量加倍，在同样的温度变化下所需热量也加倍；而相同质量的水发生同样的温度变化，所需热量是铜的 10.8 倍。前两条源于内能与热力学温度和分子数成正比；第三条是材料的性质。

concepts.name: 热量与温度变化
concepts.statement: 在没有相变且不做功的条件下，传递的热量等于质量乘以比热容再乘以温度变化。温度变化以开尔文计和以摄氏度计是相同的，所以用哪个都行；热量以千卡为单位时，比热容的单位是 kcal/(kg·°C)。这是整章的工作方程，因为之后每一种热传递方式都要回到它所产生的温度变化上来。

forms.condition: 没有相变且不做功

concepts.name: 比热容
concepts.statement: 比热容是使 1.00 kg 某种物质的温度改变 1.00 °C 所需的热量。它取决于材料及其相，一般必须查表，因为没有简单的方法可以计算它，而且对大多数固体和液体，它随温度变化不大。水的比热容是所有材料中最大的之一，是玻璃的五倍、铁的十倍，这对维持地球上的生命很重要。

concepts.name: 由功求温度升高
concepts.statement: 当功转化为内能时，把同一个方程对温度变化求解，就得到温度升高：传递的能量除以吸收它的物体的质量与比热容。卡车在下坡行驶时，刹车片把卡车失去的重力势能转化为刹车材料的内能。由于刹车片相对于卡车很小，即使只有十分之一的能量也会使它们迅速升温。

concepts.name: 量热学
concepts.statement: 当两个温度不同的物体在隔热容器中接触时，热量由较热的物体传向较冷的物体，直到它们达到共同温度。没有热量离开这一对物体，所以热物体失去的热量就是冷物体得到的热量。考虑正负号，流入冷物体的热量为正，流出热物体的热量为负，二者之和为零。这是一个量热学问题，而量热学测量食物的热含量和材料的比热容。

forms.condition: 与周围环境没有热量交换

concepts.name: 求两个物体的末温
concepts.statement: 对量热学平衡式求解末温，得到两个起始温度的加权平均，每个起始温度的权重是该物体的质量乘以比热容。150 °C 的锅与 20.0 °C 的水最终达到 59.1 °C，更接近水的温度，因为水的比热容是铝的四倍多，其质量乘以比热容是较大的权重。关键技巧是用唯一的未知温度写出失去的热量和得到的热量，然后合并各项。

forms.latex: T_{\text{f}} = \frac{m_{\text{Al}} c_{\text{Al}} T_{\text{i},\text{Al}} + m_W c_W T_{\text{i},W}}{m_{\text{Al}} c_{\text{Al}} + m_W c_W}
forms.condition: 两个物体交换热量且没有相变

concepts.name: 水对温度的调节作用
concepts.statement: 由于水的比热容比大多数常见物质大，在给定的热传递下它的温度变化很小。像湖泊这样的大片水体需要大量热量才能明显升温，所以即使气温在一天中变化很大，它的温度也几乎保持不变，而在从夏季到冬季的较长时间内它的温度确实会变化。陆地比水升温和降温更快，这正是陆风和海风的成因。

concepts.name: 潜热
concepts.statement: 物质发生相变时，热传递并不引起温度变化。能量用于破坏分子之间的内聚键，而不是增加它们的动能，所以 0 °C 的冰在全部熔化之前一直保持 0 °C。当键在凝固或凝结中重新形成时，同样的能量又释放出来，通常以热能的形式。改变一定质量的相所需的热量，等于该质量乘以潜热系数，这是一个材料常量。之所以称为潜热，即隐藏的热，是因为能量进入或离开时并不改变温度。

forms.condition: 相变期间

concepts.name: 熔化热
concepts.statement: 熔化热是使一千克物质在熔点熔化所需的热量，这一千克物质凝固时释放同样的热量。对水而言它是 334 kJ/kg，足以使一千克液态水从 0 °C 升温到 79.8 °C。因此，一袋 0 °C 的冰比同样温度的一袋水吸收的能量多得多，在喷过水的果园里，水结冰会使树木变暖。

forms.condition: 熔化或凝固
在熔点熔化

concepts.name: 汽化热
concepts.statement: 汽化热是使一千克液体在沸点变为蒸气所需的热量，蒸气凝结时释放同样的热量。对水而言它是 2256 kJ/kg，几乎是其熔化热的七倍，所以把一千克水煮干所耗的热量，比把它从冰冷升温到沸腾还多。一杯冰茶外壁上的凝结把能量释放到杯子里，加速了冰的熔化。

forms.condition: 汽化或凝结

concepts.name: 水的加热曲线
concepts.statement: 给 −20 °C 的冰加热，描出的图线有斜坡也有平台。冰升温时温度线性上升；冰熔化时停在 0 °C，每一焦耳都用于相变；然后在液态水中再次上升，但更慢，因为水的比热容是冰的两倍；水沸腾时停在 100 °C，平台长得多；之后作为蒸汽再次上升。这些平台就是潜热，把它们的长度与斜坡相比较可以看出，相变的能量比温度变化的能量大得多。

concepts.name: 沸点以下的蒸发
concepts.statement: 水在低于沸点的温度也会蒸发，而且每千克所耗的能量更多，因为分子可资利用的动能更少：在体温下汽化热为 2430 kJ/kg，比 100 °C 时约高百分之十。汗液从皮肤带走这份热量，所以出汗能降温，而高湿度减缓蒸发，汗就留在你的额头上。同样的蒸发也是潮湿气候中气温很少升到 35 °C 以上的原因。

concepts.name: 凝结和凝固释放热量
concepts.statement: 要使蒸气凝结或使液体凝固，必须移走相变在相反方向上所吸收的全部能量，周围环境接收这些能量。这就是为什么冷杯上的凝结加快了杯内冰的熔化，为什么潮湿天气里气温很少降到露点以下，为什么给果园喷水能使它免受严重霜冻，以及为什么结冰的水保持在 0 °C 而不会更冷。

concepts.name: 升华热
concepts.statement: 升华是由固相直接变为气相的转变，如雪不留一点液体痕迹地消失，干冰冒出它的烟，或霜仅由蒸气在冷窗上形成。它的发生是因为固体的平衡蒸气压不为零。所需能量是质量乘以升华热，升华热是与其他潜热同一数量级的常量，所以干冰是有效的冷却剂，而凝华释放能量。

forms.condition: 固体变为蒸气，或蒸气变为固体

concepts.name: 求有相变时的末温
concepts.statement: 当相变参与热交换时，要分阶段求解。使冰熔化的热量，再加上使熔化后的水升温的热量，与另一物体放出的热量相平衡，每一项都含有唯一的未知末温。先试着按没有相变来求解。如果温度变化会使某个物体越过熔点或沸点，就回去分步来做，并在最后检查有没有漏掉任何相变。

forms.condition: 汽水和冰不与其他任何东西交换热量

concepts.name: 热传递的三种方式
concepts.statement: 只要有温度差，就会发生热传递，而热传递的每一个过程都只通过三种方式进行：热传导、对流和辐射。三者有一个共同点，即它们传递热量仅仅是因为温度差，我们通过选择材料、控制空气的运动和选择颜色来控制它们的速率。壁炉同时显示了这三种方式。

concepts.name: 热传导
concepts.statement: 热传导是通过物理接触、经由静止物质的热传递。物质在宏观上是静止的，尽管在高于绝对零度的任何温度下，它的原子和分子都在做热运动，热量在炉灶的电热灶头与锅底之间传递，或从发热的地板传入脚掌，而没有任何东西从一处移到另一处。

concepts.name: 对流
concepts.statement: 对流是通过流体的宏观运动传递热量。流体本身把能量从一处带到另一处，如强制送风炉中的空气、烟囱中向上的气流和天气中的空气，以及汽车冷却系统中的水。

concepts.name: 辐射
concepts.statement: 通过辐射的热传递发生在微波、红外辐射、可见光或其他形式的电磁辐射被发射或吸收的时候。太阳就是这样穿过空旷的空间使地球变暖，火也主要这样使房间变暖，人体不论是否接触任何东西都会辐射红外线。

concepts.name: 分子碰撞引起的热传导
concepts.statement: 较热物体的分子平均动能较大，当一个快分子与一个慢分子在两物体接触的表面处碰撞时，能量由较快的传给较慢的。所有碰撞的累积效果，是从热物体到冷物体的净热流，它随温度差和接触面积增大，温度相等时降为零。由于依赖随机运动，热传导在大于分子作用范围的距离上是缓慢的。

concepts.name: 热传导速率
concepts.statement: 热量通过热传导流过一块材料平板的速率，正比于平板两侧的温度差和面积，反比于其厚度，并由材料的一个常量即其热导率决定。实验揭示并证实了这四个因素，无论平板是窗玻璃还是海象的皮下脂肪层，该方程都成立。它给出以瓦为单位的速率。

forms.condition: 通过平板的稳态热传导

concepts.name: 热导率
concepts.statement: 热导率衡量材料传导热量的能力，在常见物质中跨越四个以上数量级。最好的热导体银、铜、金和铝，同时也是最好的电导体，因为它们含有密度很高的自由电子，厨师使用由它们制成的器具。Styrofoam、玻璃纤维、羊毛和羽绒导热很差，因为它们截留了许多小气室，而气室中空气自身的热导率是所有物质中最低的之一。

concepts.name: R 值
concepts.statement: 良好的隔热体把小的热导率与大的厚度结合起来，厚度与热导率之比就是 R 值。热传导速率与它成反比，所以 R 值越大，隔热越好。家用隔热材料标出的就是它，而且仍用非公制单位：3.5 英寸玻璃纤维棉毡的 R 值为 11，6.5 英寸的为 19。

concepts.name: 求热传导所熔化的质量
concepts.statement: 热传导方程给出的是速率；乘以时间得到热量，这些热量可能用于相变。热车后备箱里的 Styrofoam 保温箱以由箱壁决定的速率让热量进入，一天之内这些热量所熔化的冰的质量，等于总热量除以熔化热。关键技巧是把速率换成量，再把量换成质量，并保持每一步的单位。

concepts.name: 由热流求温度差
concepts.statement: 反过来求解，热传导方程给出已知热传递速率在平板两侧所维持的温度差。通过每秒煮干一克水的锅的铝底，传过 2.26 kW，温度差只有 5.33 °C，因为铝的导热性极好；而穿过同样面积的陶瓷灶面，同样的速率则需要一千度的温度差。较小的温度差伴随较大的热流，是良导体的标志。

concepts.name: 热传导速率的比例关系
concepts.statement: 因为面积是两个长度的乘积，而厚度只是一个长度，所以把平板的每个尺寸加倍，面积变为四倍而厚度只变为两倍，热传导速率便加倍。这类比较，如薄窗与厚墙、老茧与光脚掌，都可以通过四个因素的比值来回答，而无需算出任何一个速率。

concepts.name: 自然对流
concepts.statement: 浮力驱动自然对流。受热的流体膨胀，密度降低，在周围较冷、较密的流体中上升，较冷的流体下沉来填补它的位置；所形成的环流随运动的物质携带热量。重力式热风炉以这种方式给房子供暖，炉灶上的一锅水以这种方式循环，洋流和大气也以这种方式把能量送到全球各地。强制对流，如汽车冷却系统中或皮肤的血管中的对流，是由泵驱动的同样的输运。

concepts.name: 求对流传递的热量
concepts.statement: 要求对流所携带的热量，先由密度和体积求出被移动的流体的质量，再乘以它的比热容和温度变化。除以这些质量被替换所用的时间，就得到速率。把房子里的空气升温 10.0 °C，若每半小时全部更换一次，需要 4.64 kW，相当于四十六个 100 W 灯泡的功率，这就是房屋要装防风条的原因。

forms.condition: 质量为 m 的流体在时间 t 内被移动或被替换

concepts.name: 风寒
concepts.statement: 冷风比静止的冷空气冷得多，因为对流与人体内的热传导结合起来，加快了能量离开身体的速率。风寒温度是能产生与给定温度和风速的空气相同冷却速率的静止空气的温度，它们生动地提醒我们对流传递热量的能力强于热传导：0 °C 时 15.0 m/s 的风使人感到的寒冷，就像约 −18 °C 的静止空气。

concepts.name: 被截留的空气是隔热体
concepts.statement: 空气通过对流传热很快，但热传导很差，所以它是否隔热取决于它能否流动。房屋墙体内 9 cm 的空间大到足以发生对流，因此建筑工人用隔热材料把它填满，以阻止空气运动。双层玻璃窗 1 cm 的间隙小到不能发生对流，从而利用了空气热导率低的特点。皮毛、羽毛和玻璃纤维都把空气截留在小到不能发生对流的气室里，这就是它们轻而保暖的原因。

concepts.name: 蒸发速率
concepts.statement: 当对流伴有相变时，流动的流体把潜热一起带走，带走给定功率所需的蒸发质量速率，等于该功率除以汽化热。汗液从皮肤蒸发，每分钟约 3 g，就能带走静息身体的 120 W，即使空气与皮肤一样温暖，只要气流替换掉饱和的空气。同样的过程把热量从海洋带入大气，通过正反馈把积雨云推升到平流层 20 km 的高度，也让融化的冰山冷却它漂过的海水。

forms.condition: 热量仅由蒸发带走

concepts.name: 辐射谱与温度
concepts.statement: 热物体发射不需要介质即可传播的电磁波，而且波长越短携带的能量越大。因为物体在较高温度下辐射的热量更多，所以它的颜色随温度改变：从你在尚未开始发光的炉灶加热元件上感到的红外线，到红色，再到高炉中钢的黄色和白色。理想辐射体的光谱随温度急剧上升，其峰值向可见光和紫外线移动。

concepts.name: 吸收体与发射体
concepts.statement: 辐射传热的速率主要由物体的颜色决定。黑色吸收得最好，也辐射得最好，所以黑色沥青白天比灰色人行道热，夜晚比它冷；白色和银色吸收得差，辐射得也差，像镜子一样反射辐射。理想辐射体与理想吸收体颜色相同，物体辐射进出的平衡只取决于物体自身发射和吸收得多好。

concepts.name: 发射率
concepts.statement: 发射率衡量物体辐射得多好。纯黑的理想辐射体即黑体，发射率为 1，完全反射体为 0，实际物体介于两者之间：钨丝约 0.5，炭黑约 0.99，皮肤在红外波段为 0.97，所以不论可见光下是什么颜色，我们在红外波段都近乎黑色。地球的平均发射率约为 0.65，因云量的变化而变得复杂。

concepts.name: 斯特藩-玻尔兹曼定律
terms: 辐射的斯特藩-玻尔兹曼定律
concepts.statement: 发射辐射的热传递速率等于斯特藩-玻尔兹曼常量乘以发射率，乘以表面积，再乘以以开尔文计的热力学温度的四次方。辐射速率与表面积成正比，所以把火中的炭块拨散会使站在附近明显更热；它又与温度的四次方成正比，这是极强的依赖关系，接下来的两个结果都取决于它。温度必须是热力学温度；在这个方程中代入摄氏温度值是错的。

forms.condition: T 以开尔文计

concepts.name: 辐射对四次方的依赖关系
concepts.statement: 由于辐射功率与热力学温度的四次方成正比，很小的温度差就会产生可探测的辐射差：40 °C 的物体比同一物体在 20 °C 时多辐射约 30%，34.0 °C 的皮肤比 33.0 °C 时多辐射 1.31%，足以让热像图把它显示出来。比值更大时，效应极其巨大，热力学温度为四倍的辐射体发射的功率为 256 倍。

concepts.name: 辐射的净热传递速率
concepts.statement: 所有物体都发射并吸收辐射，所以净速率是吸收减去发射；对于处在一种温度、被另一种温度的周围环境包围的物体，它是斯特藩-玻尔兹曼表达式中两个四次方之差，发射率只取物体自身的。周围是白色、灰色还是黑色都没有关系；当周围较热时，净传递是传入物体的，当周围较冷时则是传出的。一个没穿衣服的人在 22.0 °C 的房间里以这种方式损失约 99 W。

forms.condition: 温度为 T_1 的物体处在均匀温度为 T_2 的周围环境中，二者均以开尔文计

concepts.name: 温室效应
concepts.statement: 地球几乎所有能量都以太阳辐射的形式接收，并向约 3 K 的暗空辐射回去，它的稳定温度是二者的平衡。大气对太阳的可见光和大部分红外线是透明的，但较冷的地球发射的红外线波长更长，二氧化碳和水蒸气会吸收并重新辐射它，其中一部分回到地表，使地球比没有大气时约暖 40 °C。Eunice Newton Foote 最先在放在阳光下的二氧化碳烧瓶中测量到这一点，这种效应是工业和农业所排放气体引起的全球变暖的核心。

concepts.name: 求解热传递问题
concepts.statement: 要解决热传递问题，先确定起作用的是三种方式中的哪一种，再选用相应的关系式。热传导用热传导方程，热导率取自表格；对流用所携带质量的温度变化方程或潜热方程；辐射用与周围环境交换的净辐射方程。列出已知量和未知量，在代入数值之前先把方程对未知量求解，并检查答案是否合理：一个人一天之内不可能升温 36 °C，一扇窗也不可能损失 1.46 kW。

concepts.name: 斯特藩-玻尔兹曼常量
concepts.statement: 斯特藩-玻尔兹曼常量确定了给定面积、发射率和热力学温度的表面的辐射速率。其值为 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ J/(s·m²·K⁴)。

concepts.name: Restoring force
concepts.statement: When an object is displaced from its equilibrium position, the deformation creates a force in the opposite direction, which pushes the object back. Without such a force there is no oscillation, because the object would simply move in a straight line at constant speed.

concepts.name: Force constant
concepts.statement: The force constant tells how stiff a system is. The larger $\kk$ is, the greater the restoring force for the same displacement, and the stiffer the system. It is the slope of the graph of restoring force against displacement, in newtons per meter.

concepts.name: Hooke’s law
concepts.statement: The restoring force of a deformed system is directly proportional to its displacement from equilibrium and points opposite to it, $\kF = -\kk\kx$. This is Hooke’s law, and the simplest oscillations occur in systems that obey it. From the force and the displacement you can find the force constant.

forms.condition: small deformations, for which the object returns to its original shape

concepts.name: Periodic motion
concepts.statement: A motion that repeats itself at regular time intervals, such as a plucked guitar string or a mass on a spring moving up and down, is periodic. Each repetition takes the same time as the one before it, which is what makes a period and a frequency meaningful.

concepts.name: Period
concepts.statement: The period is the time to complete one oscillation. Its units are usually seconds, but may be any convenient unit of time. The word applies to the time for any event, repetitive or not, but here it is the time for one cycle of a periodic motion.

concepts.name: Frequency
concepts.statement: Frequency is the number of events per unit time. For periodic motion it is the number of oscillations per unit time, measured in hertz, where one hertz is one cycle per second. A count of cycles divided by the time they took gives the frequency, whether or not the count is made over one second.

concepts.name: Period and frequency
concepts.statement: If one cycle takes a time $\kT$, then $1/\kT$ cycles fit into each unit of time, so the frequency is the reciprocal of the period and the period is the reciprocal of the frequency. Given either one, the other follows at once.

concepts.name: Simple harmonic motion
concepts.statement: When the net force on a system can be described by Hooke’s law and there is no damping, the system oscillates with equal displacement on either side of equilibrium. This is simple harmonic motion, the simplest and most common kind of oscillation, and the system is a simple harmonic oscillator.

concepts.name: Amplitude
concepts.statement: The amplitude is the maximum displacement from equilibrium. It has the units of the displacement, meters for an object on a spring, and it is related to the energy in the oscillation. In one full period the object covers four amplitudes of ground.

concepts.name: Period of a simple harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: The period and frequency of a simple harmonic oscillator depend on the mass and the force constant alone, not on the amplitude. A stiffer system has a shorter period and a more massive one a longer period. Because the period is constant, a simple harmonic oscillator can be used as a clock.

concepts.name: Kinematics of simple harmonic motion
concepts.statement: The displacement in any simple harmonic motion is a cosine of time, $\kx(t) = \kX\cos(2\pi\kt/\kT)$. The velocity is a sine with maximum $\kvmax = 2\pi\kX/\kT = \kX\sqrt{\kk/m}$, zero at the turning points and greatest through equilibrium, and the acceleration is a cosine opposite in direction to the displacement. These are the sine waves that link simple harmonic motion to waves.

forms.latex: x = X\cos\left(\frac{2\pi t}{T}\right) = X\cos(2\pi f t)

concepts.name: Simple harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: A simple harmonic oscillator is a system that obeys Hooke’s law and so moves in simple harmonic motion, such as a mass attached to a spring.

concepts.name: Simple pendulum
concepts.statement: A simple pendulum is a small mass, the bob, hung from a light string. Displaced along its arc, it feels a net force of $-m\kg\sin\theta$ back toward the lowest point, because the tension cancels the part of the weight along the string. For small displacements it is a simple harmonic oscillator.

concepts.name: Restoring force on a pendulum
concepts.statement: For angles below about 15°, $\sin\theta$ and $\theta$ differ by 1% or less, so the restoring force $-m\kg\sin\theta$ becomes $-m\kg\theta$, and with $\ks = L\theta$ it is $-\frac{m\kg}{L}\ks$. That is Hooke’s law with a force constant $\kk = m\kg/L$, which is what makes the pendulum a simple harmonic oscillator.

concepts.name: Period of a simple pendulum
concepts.statement: Putting $\kk = m\kg/L$ into $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$ cancels the mass and leaves $\kT = 2\pi\sqrt{L/\kg}$. Only the length and the acceleration due to gravity affect the period; the mass does not, and the amplitude hardly does for small swings. This is why a pendulum keeps time.

concepts.name: Measuring g with a pendulum
concepts.statement: Squaring the period formula and solving for $\kg$ gives $\kg = 4\pi^2 L/\kT^2$. If the length is known precisely and the period is timed over many swings at a small angle, this gives the local acceleration due to gravity to several digits, which matters in geological exploration.

concepts.name: Energy of a simple harmonic oscillator
concepts.statement: A simple harmonic oscillator has no dissipative forces, so its energy is shared between elastic potential energy and kinetic energy with the total constant. The energy goes completely from one form to the other as the system oscillates: all potential at the turning points, all kinetic through equilibrium. Started from rest at $\kx = \kX$, the total is $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kX^2$.

concepts.name: Speed in simple harmonic motion
concepts.statement: Solving the conservation of energy for the velocity gives the speed at every position, greatest at equilibrium and zero at the turning points, with $\kvmax = \kX\sqrt{\kk/m}$. The maximum velocity is proportional to the amplitude, greater for stiffer systems, and smaller for larger masses.

concepts.name: Projection of uniform circular motion
concepts.statement: A point moving round a circle at constant angular velocity $\kw$ has a projection on a fixed axis at $\kx = \kX\cos\kw\kt$, and with $\kw = 2\pi/\kT$ this is exactly the position of a simple harmonic oscillator. The shadow of a ball on a turntable therefore moves in simple harmonic motion, and the speed and the period of any simple harmonic oscillator can be read off the circle: the similar triangles give $\kv = \kvmax\sqrt{1 - \kx^2/\kX^2}$, and one revolution gives $\kT = 2\pi\kX/\kvmax = 2\pi\sqrt{m/\kk}$.

concepts.name: Damped harmonic motion
concepts.statement: Completely undamped motion is rare, because friction and other non-conservative forces are seldom negligible; a guitar string stops a few seconds after you pluck it. With a little damping, the period and frequency stay nearly those of simple harmonic motion, but the amplitude gradually decreases as the damping force removes energy, usually as thermal energy. More damping opposes and slows the motion, so the period and frequency begin to change. With very large damping the system does not oscillate at all.

concepts.name: Energy removed by damping
concepts.statement: Energy removal by non-conservative forces is described by $\kWnc = \Delta(\kKE + \kPEtot)$, where $\kWnc$ is the work done by the non-conservative force, here the damping force. For a damped harmonic oscillator this work is negative, because it removes mechanical energy from the system, so the mechanical energy of a damped oscillator can only fall with time.

concepts.name: Critical damping
concepts.statement: Critical damping returns an oscillator to its equilibrium position as quickly as possible. A critically damped system may overshoot the equilibrium position, but if it does, it will do so only once. Car suspensions and bathroom scales use it, because the system returns to equilibrium rapidly and stays there. A constant force moves it to a new equilibrium in the shortest possible time without oscillation.

concepts.name: Underdamping
concepts.statement: With less than critical damping, the system returns toward equilibrium faster than a critically damped one but overshoots and crosses the equilibrium position one or more times, its amplitude gradually decreasing to zero. Such a system is underdamped, and the lightly damped oscillator whose amplitude slowly decays while its period stays almost the same is the common case.

concepts.name: Overdamping
concepts.statement: An overdamped system, curve B, returns to equilibrium without oscillating, and does so over a longer time than a critically damped one; like the critically damped system it may overshoot, but it reaches equilibrium slowly. Heavy damping is wanted where small-amplitude motion matters more than a quick return, and its cost is the slowness.

concepts.name: Finding the travel of a friction-damped oscillator
concepts.statement: When the damping is simple friction, the work it does is $-\kff\kd$, with $\kff = \mu_{\text{k}} m\kg$ and $\kd$ the total distance travelled, and the motion stops where the friction balances the force of the spring, at $\kx = \mu_{\text{k}} m\kg/\kk$. Equating the work done by friction to the change in stored elastic energy gives the total distance the object travels before it stops. This is an integrated concepts problem: friction from Newton's laws, then work and the conservation of energy.

forms.condition: an object released from rest at X on a horizontal spring with simple friction
where the object stops, the friction balancing the force of the spring
simple friction between the object and the surface

concepts.name: Natural frequency
concepts.statement: The natural frequency is the frequency at which a system would oscillate if there were no driving and no damping force. Objects can be forced to oscillate, but they oscillate best at their natural frequency; a piano's strings sing back the note you sing at them because their frequencies match your voice.

concepts.name: Resonance
concepts.statement: Driving a system at its natural frequency is called resonance, and the system is said to resonate. Drive a paddle ball at its natural frequency and its amplitude grows with each oscillation for as long as you drive it. At driving frequencies well above or below, the ball takes up energy less efficiently and oscillates with a smaller amplitude. Radios, MRI, a child on a swing and the Tacoma Narrows Bridge all show resonance.

concepts.name: Resonance curve and damping
concepts.statement: The amplitude of a driven, damped harmonic oscillator peaks where the driving frequency equals the natural frequency, whatever the damping. The least damping gives the highest and narrowest peak, because the damping force removes the least energy. A piano string or a radio, which must resonate at one precise frequency, needs as little damping as possible. A car’s suspension needs heavy damping, which lowers the amplitude but lets it respond over more frequencies.

concepts.name: Finding the energy a damper removes
concepts.statement: The energy a shock absorber must dissipate to damp a bounce is the mechanical energy of the oscillation, $\tfrac{1}{2}m\kv^2$ at the equilibrium position or $\tfrac{1}{2}\kk\kX^2$ at maximum displacement, and the energy a driving force must supply to raise an amplitude is the difference between two such stores. At resonance the driver puts energy in at a steady rate, so the time to reach a larger amplitude is that difference divided by the rate.

concepts.name: Wave
concepts.statement: A wave is a disturbance that propagates, or moves from the place it was created. For water waves the disturbance is in the surface of the water, for sound it is a change in air pressure, and for earthquakes it is the ground itself. The simplest waves repeat for several cycles and go with simple harmonic motion. A gull bobs up and down as the crests and troughs pass under it, while the wave itself, the disturbance and not the water, moves on.

concepts.name: Wave velocity
concepts.statement: The wave velocity is the speed at which the disturbance moves, sometimes called the propagation velocity or propagation speed. It is the speed of the wave, not the speed at which the gull moves up and down: for water waves it is the speed of a surface wave, for sound the speed of sound, for visible light the speed of light.

concepts.name: Wavelength
concepts.statement: The wavelength is the distance between adjacent identical parts of a wave, measured parallel to the direction of propagation. The size of the disturbance, its amplitude, is a different length and is completely independent of the speed of propagation.

concepts.name: Wave speed, wavelength and frequency
concepts.statement: The speed of propagation is the distance the wave travels in a given time, which is one wavelength in the time of one period, so $\kvw = \klam/\kT$, or $\kvw = \kf\klam$. This fundamental relationship holds for all types of waves: water waves, sound and light alike.

concepts.name: Transverse wave
concepts.statement: In a transverse, or shear, wave the disturbance is perpendicular to the direction of propagation: the cord is moved up and down while the wave travels horizontally along it. The waves on the strings of musical instruments are transverse, and so are electromagnetic waves such as visible light.

concepts.name: Longitudinal wave
concepts.statement: In a longitudinal, or compressional, wave the disturbance is parallel to the direction of propagation: the cord is pushed and pulled along its own length. Sound waves in air and water are longitudinal, because fluids have no appreciable shear strength and so can carry only periodic variations in pressure; sound in solids, and earthquake waves, can be both longitudinal and transverse.

concepts.name: Superposition
concepts.statement: When two or more waves arrive at the same point, their disturbances are superimposed on one another. Each disturbance corresponds to a force, and forces add, so if the disturbances are along the same line the resulting wave is a simple addition of the disturbances of the individual waves: their amplitudes add. Most waves look complex because they are several simple waves added together, and the rules for adding them are this simple.

forms.condition: disturbances along the same line

concepts.name: Constructive interference
concepts.statement: Two identical waves that arrive at the same point exactly in phase, crest aligned with crest and trough with trough, produce pure constructive interference: a wave with twice the amplitude of the individual waves but the same wavelength. It is one end of what superposition can do, and most real superpositions are a mixture of it and its opposite that varies from place to place and time to time.

concepts.name: Destructive interference
concepts.statement: Two identical waves that arrive exactly out of phase, precisely aligned crest to trough, produce pure destructive interference: the disturbances are in opposite directions and the resulting amplitude is zero, so the waves completely cancel. Sound from a stereo that is loud in one spot and quiet in another is the two kinds of interference at different places in the same room.

concepts.name: Standing wave
concepts.statement: Two identical waves moving in opposite directions superimpose to a wave that stands in place. They alternate between constructive and destructive interference as they move through each other, and the resultant oscillates at fixed locations without travelling. The waves on a glass of milk in a refrigerator, on guitar strings and in organ pipes are standing waves, formed by reflections from the sides or the ends.

concepts.name: Nodes and antinodes
concepts.statement: Nodes are the points where the string does not move; more generally, nodes are where the wave disturbance is zero in a standing wave. The fixed ends of a string must be nodes, because the string cannot move there. An antinode is the location of maximum amplitude in a standing wave.

concepts.name: Fundamental and overtones of a string
concepts.statement: On a string fixed at both ends the longest wavelength is $\klamone = 2L$, so the lowest frequency, the fundamental, is $\kfone = \kvw/\klamone = \kvw/2L$. The overtones, or harmonics, are multiples of the fundamental: $\klamtwo = L$ gives $\kftwo = 2\kfone$, and $\kfthree = 3\kfone$, and so on. Raise the tension and all of these frequencies rise together, because greater tension means a greater $\kvw$. That is how a string instrument is tuned.

forms.condition: a string fixed at both ends
a string fixed at both ends
a string fixed at both ends

concepts.name: Beats
concepts.statement: The superposition of two waves of similar but not identical frequencies goes in and out of phase, alternately constructive and destructive, so the resultant has the average frequency of the two and an amplitude that rises and falls: it beats. Two adjacent piano keys warble and the twin engines of a taxiing jet swell and fade for this reason, and the product form $\kx = 2\kX\cos(\pi\kfB\kt)\cos(2\pi\kfave\kt)$ shows the slow cosine that carries the amplitude and the fast one that is the wave.

forms.condition: two waves of identical amplitude and similar frequency

forms.latex: x = X\cos(2\pi f_1 t) + X\cos(2\pi f_2 t)

concepts.name: Beat frequency
concepts.statement: The frequency at which the amplitude of the resultant fluctuates is the beat frequency, the absolute value of the difference of the two frequencies. It is the same for all types of waves; for sound, provided the two frequencies are similar, what is heard is the average frequency getting louder and softer at the beat frequency. Listening for beats is a very useful way to compare similar frequencies, which is how a piano is tuned against a fork.

concepts.name: Wave energy and amplitude
concepts.statement: All waves carry energy, and the amount depends on the amplitude. A wave is a displacement resisted by a restoring force, so the larger the displacement $\kx$, the larger the force $\kF = \kk\kx$ needed to create it. The work done to create the wave supplies its energy, so $\kW \propto \kF\kx = \kk\kx^2$. The intensity, an energy per unit time and area, is also proportional to the amplitude squared. Two identical waves that interfere perfectly constructively therefore have four times the intensity of one, not twice.

concepts.name: Intensity
concepts.statement: Intensity is defined as power per unit area, $\kIntens = \kP/A$, where $\kP$ is the power carried by the wave through the area $A$; its SI unit is the watt per square metre. The definition is valid for any energy in transit, including that carried by waves. It gathers the three things the energy effects of a wave depend on, the amplitude, the time and the area the wave covers: sunlight arrives above the atmosphere at 1300 W/m², and a 90 decibel sound is only 10⁻³ W/m².

concepts.name: Finding energy from intensity
concepts.statement: Because power is energy per unit time, $\kP = \kE/\kt$, the definition of intensity becomes $\kIntens = (\kE/\kt)/A$, and you can solve it for the energy, $\kE = \kIntens A\kt$, or for the time. The longer a wave acts and the larger the area it falls on, the more energy it delivers. That is why a deep-heat ultrasound treatment has a set time and a solar collector a set size.

concepts.name: Concentrating or spreading a wave
concepts.statement: Focusing or spreading a wave changes the area it covers, which changes the intensity while the power stays the same. Take the ratio of the new intensity to the old, with primes for the new quantities. The powers cancel, so the ratio of intensities is the inverse ratio of the areas. Sunlight focused by a magnifying glass onto an area 200 times smaller is 200 times as intense, enough to start a fire.

forms.condition: the same power through both areas, P' = P

concepts.name: Electric charge
concepts.statement: A physical quantity not previously introduced, electric charge, explains the effects of static electricity. There are only two types of charge, one called positive and the other called negative. We know there are two because rubbing certain materials together in controlled ways always produces one type on one material and the opposite type on the other. Glass rubbed with silk becomes positive and the silk negative, and the names are a convention that goes back to Franklin.

concepts.name: Like charges repel
concepts.statement: Two glass rods rubbed with silk repel one another, since each carries positive charge, and two silk cloths so rubbed repel too, while the rod and the silk attract because their charges are opposite. The force between charges decreases with distance. These two facts explain static cling, the balloon on the wall and the hair that stands on end. Coulomb’s law will later say exactly how the force depends on the charges and their separation.

concepts.name: Charges of the electron and proton
concepts.statement: Normal matter is made of atoms, and atoms contain positive and negative charges, usually in equal amounts. In the planetary model, negative electrons orbit a much heavier positive nucleus whose charge is due to its protons; the neutron carries no charge. Nearly all charge in nature is due to electrons and protons, whose charges are identical in magnitude but opposite in sign, and the other charged particles seen in cosmic rays and accelerators survive only a short time.

concepts.name: Elementary charge
concepts.statement: All charged objects in nature are integral multiples of one basic quantity of charge, the magnitude of the charge on a single electron or proton, $|q_\text{e}| = 1.60 \times 10^{-19}$ C. The symbol $q$ stands for charge, and the subscript e marks the charge of a single electron or proton. No directly observed charge is smaller than this. The quarks inside a proton carry $-\tfrac13$ and $+\tfrac23$ of it, but no one has ever seen a quark alone.

concepts.name: Counting the charges in a charge
concepts.statement: The SI unit of charge is the coulomb, and the number of protons needed to make 1.00 C is $6.25 \times 10^{18}$, one coulomb divided by the charge on one proton. The same number of electrons carries $-1.00$ C. To turn any charge into a count of electrons, divide by $|q_\text{e}|$. To turn a count of electrons moved through a wire or removed from a neutral object back into coulombs, multiply.

concepts.name: Rubbing separates existing charge
concepts.statement: Rubbing materials together separates charges in atoms and molecules. Some atoms and molecules have a greater affinity for electrons than others and become negatively charged by close contact, leaving the other material positively charged. Batteries separate charge by chemical interactions instead. Separating charges in this way creates and destroys none; it only moves existing charges about. For macroscopic objects, negatively charged means an excess of electrons and positively charged a depletion of them.

concepts.name: Conservation of charge
concepts.statement: Total charge is constant in any process. Rubbing only moves existing charge about. Even in a particle accelerator, where energy becomes mass in the amount $\Delta m = E/c^2$, every charged particle appears together with another of opposite charge, so the total charge created is zero. When a particle and its antimatter counterpart annihilate, the total charge is zero before and after. No experiment has ever found the law violated. Charge joins energy, momentum and angular momentum on the short list of quantities that nature always conserves.

concepts.name: Static electricity
concepts.statement: Static electricity is a buildup of electric charge on the surface of an object. It is what makes a comb rubbed through dry hair attract bits of paper and a sock cling to a sweater from the dryer.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic force
concepts.statement: The electromagnetic force is one of the four basic forces of nature. It consists of the static electric forces between charges, the magnetic forces between moving charges and magnets, and the electromagnetic waves that carry them through space.

concepts.name: Electron
concepts.statement: The electron is a particle orbiting the nucleus of an atom and carrying the smallest unit of negative charge.

concepts.name: Proton
concepts.statement: The proton is a particle in the nucleus of an atom carrying a positive charge equal in magnitude to the charge of the electron, and it is far more massive.

concepts.name: Conductor
concepts.statement: Some substances, such as metals and salty water, allow charges to move through them with relative ease. Some of the electrons in metals are not bound to individual atoms, and these free electrons can move through the material much as air moves through loose sand; salty water and similar materials contain free ions instead, an ion being an atom or molecule with a nonzero total charge. Any substance that has free electrons or free ions and allows charge to move relatively freely through it is a conductor.

concepts.name: Insulator
concepts.statement: Other substances, such as glass, do not allow charges to move through them; these are insulators. Electrons and ions in insulators are bound in the structure and cannot move easily, as much as $10^{23}$ times more slowly than in conductors. Pure water and dry table salt are insulators, whereas molten salt and salty water are conductors, and the rubber and plastic round a wire keep its charge from escaping outward.

concepts.name: Charging by contact
concepts.statement: Touching an object with a charged object charges it with the same sign. When a positively charged glass rod touches the ball of an electroscope, the rod attracts electrons to the top of the electroscope and some pass to the rod. The electroscope keeps a net positive charge, whose repulsion separates the light gold leaves, and the rod loses some of its excess charge in the transfer. Because the rod is an insulator, it must actually touch the electroscope to transfer charge.

concepts.name: Polarization
concepts.statement: Polarization is the separation of charges in an object that remains neutral. When a charged rod comes near a neutral conductor, it attracts charge of the opposite sign to the near side and leaves like charge on the far side. In an insulator the distribution of charge in each atom or molecule shifts slightly. Some molecules, like water, are polar, with a natural separation of charge although they are neutral overall.

concepts.name: Grounding
concepts.statement: A conductor is grounded when a conducting wire runs from it to the ground. Since the earth is large and most ground is a good conductor, it can supply or accept excess charge easily. A grounded conductor loses any excess charge to the earth, or draws from it whatever a nearby charge attracts. Breaking the ground connection before you remove a nearby charged object leaves the conductor with a net charge.

concepts.name: Charging by induction
concepts.statement: You can charge an object without transferring excess charge to it directly. A charged rod brought near two touching neutral spheres attracts opposite charge to the near sphere and leaves the other with like charge. Separate the spheres before you pull the rod away, and each keeps a net charge. You can charge a single sphere the same way by grounding it while the rod is near, then breaking the ground connection. The object charged by induction receives the opposite charge to the rod, and the rod loses none of its excess charge, so you can repeat the process.

concepts.name: Attraction of neutral objects
concepts.statement: Any charged object, positive or negative, attracts neutral objects. When a charged rod comes near a neutral substance, it attracts opposite charge nearer and repels like charge. The electrostatic force decreases with distance, so the repulsion of the like charges, which are farther away, is weaker than the attraction of the unlike charges, which are nearer. The net force is an attraction. That is why polished amber picks up straw, a comb picks up paper, and a charged rod bends a stream of water.

concepts.name: Free charge
concepts.statement: A free charge is an electric charge that can move about separately from its atom or molecule. In metals some electrons are not bound to individual atoms, and these free electrons carry charge through the material.

concepts.name: Free electron
concepts.statement: A free electron is an electron that is free to move away from its atomic orbit. Metals are good conductors because some of their electrons are free.

concepts.name: Electrostatic repulsion
concepts.statement: Electrostatic repulsion is the phenomenon of two objects with like charges repelling each other.

concepts.name: Coulomb’s law
concepts.statement: The main features of the electrostatic force are two types of charge, like charges repelling and unlike attracting, and the decrease of the force with distance. In the late eighteenth century Charles Coulomb turned them into the formula named for him. Coulomb’s law gives the magnitude of the force between two point charges separated by a distance $r$. It is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. Modern experiments have verified the inverse square to one part in $10^{16}$ and found no exception, even within the atom.

forms.condition: two point charges

concepts.name: Coulomb’s constant
concepts.statement: In SI units the constant in Coulomb’s law is $k = 8.988 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2/\text{C}^2$, usually rounded to $8.99 \times 10^{9}$. Its size is what makes a coulomb such a large amount of charge: two charges of 1 C each, held 1 m apart, would push on one another with a force of nearly $10^{10}$ N, which is why the charges of everyday static electricity are nanocoulombs and microcoulombs.

concepts.name: Direction of the Coulomb force
concepts.statement: The electrostatic force is a vector quantity expressed in newtons, and it is understood to be along the line joining the two charges, repulsive for like charges and attractive for unlike. Newton’s third law applies as usual: the force on $q_1$ is equal in magnitude and opposite in direction to the force $q_1$ exerts on $q_2$, whatever the sizes of the two charges.

concepts.name: Scaling the Coulomb force
concepts.statement: Because the force is proportional to each charge and inversely proportional to the square of the separation, a change in any one of them changes the force by a factor that can be read off without evaluating the constant. Halving the distance multiplies the force by four, tripling it divides by nine, doubling one charge doubles the force, and a change of the force by a factor of 10 needs a change of the distance by $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.2$ either way.

concepts.name: Coulomb force versus gravity
concepts.statement: For an electron and a proton the ratio of the electrostatic force to the gravitational force is $2.27 \times 10^{39}$, at any separation, since both fall off as the inverse square and the distance cancels in the ratio. Gravity is therefore completely negligible where individual charged particles interact. On a large scale the reverse is true: most objects are nearly electrically neutral, so the attractive and repulsive Coulomb forces nearly cancel, while gravity, which is always attractive, adds up and dominates between large objects.

forms.condition: an electron and a proton, at any separation

concepts.name: Electrostatic force
concepts.statement: The electrostatic force, also called the Coulomb force, is the attraction or repulsion between two charged bodies, with both a magnitude and a direction. Coulomb's law gives it for point charges.

concepts.name: Coulomb force field
concepts.statement: A field maps the force that surrounds any object and acts on another object at a distance without apparent physical connection, as the gravitational field of the earth maps the force a mass would feel at any point. The Coulomb force field surrounding a charge $Q$ extends throughout space, and Coulomb’s law gives its magnitude as $F = k|qQ|/r^2$ on a test charge $q$. Both its magnitude and its direction depend on the test charge as well as on $Q$, so it is not unique at any point in space.

concepts.name: Point charge and test charge
concepts.statement: The charge that creates a field is a point charge, written $Q$, and the charge set down in the field to feel it is a test charge, written $q$. The test charge is taken to be positive, so that the field has the direction of the force on it, and so small that it does not alter the charge distribution creating the field.

concepts.name: Electric field
concepts.statement: To have a field that depends only on the charge creating it, the electric field is defined as the ratio of the Coulomb force to the positive test charge it acts on. So defined, it represents only the charge creating it and is unique at every point in space, its direction is the direction of the force on a positive test charge, and its units are newtons per coulomb. It is a vector, and fields due to several charges add like vectors.

concepts.name: Force on a charge in a field
concepts.statement: If the electric field is known, the electrostatic force on any charge $q$ is obtained by multiplying the charge by the field. The force on a positive charge is in the direction of the field, and the force on a negative charge is opposite to it, which is what a negative sign on $q$ says.

concepts.name: Field of a point charge
concepts.statement: Applying the definition of the field to Coulomb’s force on a test charge, the test charge cancels and the magnitude of the electric field of a point charge is $E = k|Q|/r^2$. The field depends only on the charge $Q$ and the distance $r$ from it, and is completely independent of the test charge; it points away from a positive $Q$ and toward a negative one.

forms.condition: a point charge
point charge

concepts.name: Direction of the electric field
concepts.statement: Because the field is defined for a positive test charge, it points away from a positive charge and toward a negative charge, and the force on a charge placed in it is along the field for a positive charge and against it for a negative one. A field found to be positive in a calculation is a field pointing away from the charge that creates it.

concepts.name: Point charge
concepts.statement: A point charge, designated $Q$, is a charged particle that generates an electric field.

concepts.name: Electric field lines
concepts.statement: Since the electric field has both magnitude and direction, it is a vector, and you can draw it at any point as an arrow whose length is its magnitude. The standard picture replaces the arrows with continuous field lines that have the same direction at any point as the field, and the closeness of the lines shows the strength of the field. Field lines are a map of infinitesimal force vectors, a pictorial tool and not a physical entity. Gravitational, magnetic and other fields use the same picture.

concepts.name: Properties of electric field lines
concepts.statement: For any charge distribution, field lines begin on positive charges and end on negative charges, or at infinity for an isolated charge. The number of lines leaving a positive charge or entering a negative one is proportional to the magnitude of the charge. The strength of the field is proportional to the number of lines per unit area perpendicular to them. The field of a point charge falls as $1/r^2$, and its lines spread over an area that grows as $r^2$, so they show it exactly. The direction of the field is tangent to the line at any point. Field lines can never cross, since the field is unique at every point and a crossing would give it two directions.

concepts.name: Superposition of electric fields
concepts.statement: In many situations there are multiple charges, and the total electric field they create at a point is the vector sum of the individual fields created by each charge. The field of each charge at the point is found from $E = k|Q|/r^2$ with the direction of the force on a positive test charge there, and the fields are then added with the same vector techniques used for forces and velocities.

concepts.name: Adding the fields of two charges
concepts.statement: To find the total field at a point, find the field of each charge there in magnitude and direction, pretending a positive test charge sits at the point to fix the directions, then add the vectors. When the two fields are perpendicular, as in Example 18.4, the Pythagorean theorem gives the magnitude and the inverse tangent gives the direction; otherwise components or graphical techniques are used.

forms.condition: two perpendicular fields
two perpendicular fields

concepts.name: Finding the total force from several charges
concepts.statement: The total force on a charge is the vector sum of the Coulomb forces the other charges exert on it, each along the line joining the pair and each found from Coulomb’s law. Equivalently, it is the charge multiplied by the total electric field at its position. Symmetry often settles the direction before you enter any number, and the net force is zero wherever the individual forces cancel.

concepts.name: Field of two charges
concepts.statement: The field of two point charges can be drawn by finding the total field at representative points and drawing lines consistent with them. Between two like charges the field is weaker, the lines farther apart, because the fields of the two charges oppose one another there, and at a great distance the field becomes that of a single larger charge. Between two unlike charges the field is stronger, since the two fields point the same way, and at large distances it is weak, since the two fields subtract, looking like the field of a smaller single charge.

concepts.name: Sketching electric field lines
concepts.statement: A field-line drawing is built from the five properties: lines leave positive charges and enter negative ones in numbers proportional to the charges, they never cross, their direction is the field’s and their closeness is its strength. Near a single charge the lines are radial, near two charges they bend as Figures 18.22 and 18.23 show, and far from any distribution they look like the lines of one charge equal to the total.

concepts.name: Large biological molecules are charged
concepts.statement: Classical electrostatics has an important role in molecular biology, because the large molecules so important to life, proteins and nucleic acids, are usually electrically charged. DNA carries about two fundamental charges per 0.3 nm along its length, and it is the electrostatic force that holds the molecule together and gives it its structure and strength; since the Coulomb force falls as $1/r^2$, the base pairs must be close enough, about 0.3 nm within a base and 1 nm between the strands, for the force to hold them.

concepts.name: Polar molecules and dipoles
concepts.statement: Water is a strongly polar molecule: its ten electrons tend to remain closer to the oxygen nucleus than to the hydrogen nuclei, which creates two centers of equal and opposite charge, a dipole, whose magnitude is the dipole moment. The oxygen side is slightly negative and the hydrogen ends slightly positive, and the attraction of opposite charges between molecules follows. A molecule with a natural separation of charge is more strongly affected by other charges than one with a uniform distribution.

concepts.name: Electrostatic screening
concepts.statement: Many molecules in living things are charged, yet electrostatic forces play a smaller role in biology than you might expect, because screening dilutes them. The two centers of charge in a water molecule, and the Na⁺, K⁺ and Cl⁻ ions inside and outside cells, end some of the field lines coming from a free charge and weaken the Coulomb interaction. Screening makes the Coulomb force a short-range force rather than a long-range one. Microtubules within a cell may still extend electric fields over larger distances.

concepts.name: Dipole
concepts.statement: A dipole is a pair of separated centers of equal and opposite charge, such as a molecule whose charge is not symmetrically distributed, so that one side is more positive and the other more negative.

concepts.name: Electrostatic equilibrium
concepts.statement: Conductors contain free charges that move easily. When you place excess charge on a conductor or put it in a static electric field, the charges quickly reach a steady state called electrostatic equilibrium. The free charges move until no force remains to move them, and every property of a conductor in equilibrium follows from that condition. In metals the free charges are electrons, but a positive charge moving one way is equivalent to a negative charge moving the other.

concepts.name: Field at the surface of a conductor
concepts.statement: There can be no component of the field parallel to the surface of a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium, since if there were it would exert a force $F_\parallel = qE_\parallel$ on the free charges and produce further movement of charge. The free charges move until the field is perpendicular to the surface, so just outside a conductor the field lines are perpendicular to it, ending or beginning on charges on the surface.

concepts.name: Field inside a conductor
concepts.statement: An electric field polarizes a conductor placed in it. Its free charges move until the field lines end on excess negative charge on one part of the surface and begin again on excess positive charge on the opposite side. No field remains inside, since free charges would keep moving in response to any field until they cancelled it. The field outside becomes stronger near the conductor and disappears entirely within it.

concepts.name: Excess charge on a conductor’s surface
concepts.statement: Excess charges on a spherical conductor repel one another and move until they spread evenly over its surface, where they stay once the field inside is zero. Any excess charge resides entirely on the surface or surfaces of a conductor. Outside a charged sphere the field is exactly that of a point charge at its center equal to the excess charge.

concepts.name: Field between parallel plates
concepts.statement: Two metal plates with equal and opposite excess charges create a very uniform electric field. The properties of conductors in equilibrium spread the charges uniformly except near the edges. The field lines are therefore uniformly spaced, so the field is uniform in strength, and perpendicular to the flat surfaces, so it is uniform in direction. The edge effects matter less when the plates are close together. Such a field gives charges a uniform acceleration, as in the electron gun of an old cathode-ray tube.

concepts.name: Earth’s electric field
concepts.statement: A near-uniform electric field of about 150 N/C, directed downward, surrounds Earth, maintained in fair weather between the positive ionosphere, a layer of charged particles about 100 km up, and the largely negative Earth, both of which are conductors. In storm conditions clouds form and local fields can be larger and reversed; if the field exceeds about $3 \times 10^{6}$ N/C the insulating air breaks down and becomes conducting, and the discharge is lightning or corona.

concepts.name: Charge concentration at points
concepts.statement: On a nonuniform conductor the excess charges become concentrated at the sharpest points. The forces between identical pairs of charges at either end of the conductor are the same, but only the component parallel to the surface moves charge apart. That component is greatest on the flattest surface and smallest at the most pointed end, so the charges end up closer together at the point. The field, which must meet the surface at right angles, is strongest there. An external field polarizes a conductor the same way, with its most concentrated charge at its most pointed end.

concepts.name: Lightning rods and smooth conductors
concepts.statement: On a very sharply curved surface the charges are so concentrated that the field can pull them off the surface. Lightning rods work best when they are most pointed, because the point continually bleeds away the charge a storm cloud induces on a building and so prevents the more dramatic strike. To prevent the transfer of charge instead, as on a high-voltage transmission line or the terminal of a Van de Graaff generator, make the conductor very smooth, with as large a radius of curvature as possible.

concepts.name: Faraday cage
concepts.statement: A Faraday cage is a metal shield that encloses a volume: all electrical charges reside on its outside surface and there is no electric field inside, so it keeps stray fields in the environment from interfering with sensitive measurements such as the signals inside a nerve cell. A car’s metal body is a Faraday cage, which is why it is best to stay inside it during an electrical storm or if a live wire has fallen on it, provided you remain totally inside.

concepts.name: Ionosphere
concepts.statement: The ionosphere is a layer of charged particles about 100 km above the surface of Earth. It is positive, and with the largely negative Earth it maintains the fair-weather electric field.

concepts.name: Van de Graaff generator
concepts.statement: A Van de Graaff generator uses both smooth and pointed surfaces, and conductors and insulators, to build large static charges and hence large voltages. A pointed conductor sprays charge onto a moving insulating belt near the bottom. A second pointed conductor inside the large sphere picks it off at the top, and the charge moves to the sphere’s outside surface. A very large excess charge builds up before the field polarizes and ionizes the surrounding material and lets it escape. Van de Graaff built the first in 1931 for nuclear physics research, and voltages of 15 million volts are practical.

concepts.name: Xerography and the laser printer
concepts.statement: Most copy machines use xerography, a dry copying process based on electrostatics. Points spray positive charge onto a selenium-coated aluminum drum. Selenium is a photoconductor, an insulator in the dark and a conductor in the light, so where the image is light the charge leaks away to the grounded drum, and where it is dark the positive charge remains. The charged regions attract negatively charged toner. A paper given a greater positive charge pulls the toner off the drum, and heated rollers melt it into the fibers. A laser printer makes the image on the drum with a scanned laser beam and is otherwise the same process.

concepts.name: Ink jet printer
concepts.statement: An ink jet printer makes a fine spray of tiny ink droplets and gives them an electrostatic charge. Pairs of charged plates then direct them with great precision to form letters and images on paper, and a black jet and three colored jets produce color. Electrostatic painting charges paint the same way. Mutual repulsion of like charges makes the paint fly from its source, and surface tension forms drops. The unlike charge of the surface draws them in, perpendicular to a conductor and with extra paint on corners and points.

concepts.name: Electrostatic precipitators and air cleaning
concepts.statement: An electrostatic air cleaner places excess charge, usually positive, on the smoke, dust, pollen and other particles in the air and then passes the air through an oppositely charged grid that attracts and retains them. Large precipitators remove over 99% of the particles from the stack gas of coal- and oil-fired plants, and home units remove polluting particles, irritants and allergens.

concepts.name: Solving electrostatics problems
concepts.statement: First examine the situation to see whether static electricity plays a part. Identify the system with the number, locations and types of charges. List the unknowns and decide whether you need the Coulomb force directly; if so, a free-body diagram drawn with field lines helps. List the knowns, keeping the Coulomb force $F$ distinct from the electric field $E$. Solve the appropriate equation or draw the field lines. Then check the answer for reasonable size, sign and units. An unreasonable answer usually points to the premise that produced it, such as an excessively large separated charge.

concepts.name: Joining electrostatics to Newton’s laws
concepts.statement: The electric field exerts a force on charges, and so the problems of electrostatics reach into dynamics, kinematics, circular motion, statics and fluids. The strategy is to identify the physical principles involved and the chapters they come from, then solve each part with that part’s own strategy: weight from $w = mg$, the electric force from $F = qE$, the acceleration from Newton’s second law with the net force, and the motion that follows from the kinematics of constant acceleration.

concepts.name: Electrostatics
concepts.statement: Electrostatics is the study of electric forces that are static or slow-moving. Its ideas are put to work in machines such as the Van de Graaff generator, the copier and the electrostatic precipitator.

concepts.name: Photoconductor
concepts.statement: A photoconductor is a substance that is an insulator until it is exposed to light, when it becomes a conductor. Selenium is one.

concepts.name: Laser printer
concepts.statement: A laser printer uses a laser to create a photoconductive image on a drum, which attracts dry ink particles that are then rolled onto paper.

concepts.name: Sound
