concepts.statement: Sound is a disturbance of matter that is transmitted from its source outward, and it is a wave. On the atomic scale it is a disturbance of atoms that is far more ordered than their thermal motions, and in many instances it is a periodic wave in which the atoms undergo simple harmonic motion.

concepts.name: Sound as a pressure wave
concepts.statement: A vibrating string compresses the air in front of it and expands the air behind it, and these compressions and rarefactions move out as longitudinal pressure waves with the frequency of the string. Sound waves in air and most fluids are longitudinal because fluids have almost no shear strength. A graph of gauge pressure against distance from the source is a sine wave, and for ordinary sounds the pressure varies only slightly from atmospheric. The amplitude decreases with distance for three reasons. The energy spreads over a larger area, objects such as the eardrum absorb it, and the viscosity of air and heat transfer between compressions and rarefactions turn it into thermal motion.

concepts.name: Hearing
concepts.statement: Hearing is the perception of sound, just as vision is the perception of visible light. The physical phenomenon and its perception are related but not the same thing, and the chapter keeps them apart: wavelength, frequency, amplitude and speed of propagation belong to the wave, and pitch and loudness belong to the listener.

concepts.name: Pitch
concepts.statement: Perception of frequency is called pitch. You sense the frequency of a sound directly, and the wavelength only indirectly, through the size of a musical instrument. Small instruments such as a piccolo make high-pitch, short-wavelength sounds, and large instruments such as a tuba make low-pitch, long-wavelength ones.

concepts.name: Speed of sound, frequency and wavelength
concepts.statement: The relationship of the speed of sound, its frequency and its wavelength is the same as for all waves. The wavelength is the distance between adjacent identical parts of the wave, for example between adjacent compressions, and the frequency is that of the source, the number of waves that pass a point per unit time. In a given medium under fixed conditions the speed is constant, so the higher the frequency, the smaller the wavelength.

concepts.name: Speed of sound in different media
concepts.statement: The speed of sound in a medium is determined by a combination of the medium's rigidity, or compressibility in gases, and its density. The more rigid or less compressible the medium, the faster the speed of sound, and for materials of similar rigidity sound travels faster through the one with the lower density. The speed of sound in air is low because air is compressible, and it is generally greater in liquids and solids. Earthquakes show the same dependence: longitudinal P-waves outrun transverse S-waves in granite because its bulk modulus is greater than its shear modulus.

concepts.name: Speed of sound and temperature
concepts.statement: For air at sea level the speed of sound is 331 m/s at 0 °C and grows as the square root of the kelvin temperature. The speed of sound in a gas follows the average speed of its particles, which itself goes as the square root of the temperature. The dependence is real but not strong: at 20.0 °C the speed is 343 m/s, less than a 4% increase.

forms.condition: air at sea level, T in kelvin

concepts.name: Speed of sound and frequency
concepts.statement: In open air the speed of sound is the same for all frequencies in the audible range. If it were not, the music of a marching band would arrive out of cadence, the low-pitch instruments lagging the high-pitch ones more the farther away you stood; because all instruments arrive together at any distance, all frequencies travel at nearly the same speed, and so a fixed speed ties frequency and wavelength together.

concepts.name: Frequency across media
concepts.statement: When sound travels from one medium to another its speed changes, but its frequency usually remains the same, because it is like a driven oscillation and has the frequency of the original source. Since the speed changes and the frequency does not, the wavelength must change: the higher the speed of sound, the greater the wavelength for a given frequency.

concepts.name: Finding a distance from an echo
concepts.statement: A bat uses sound echoes to find its way about and to catch prey, and sonar and medical imaging use them the same way. The sound travels out and back at the speed of sound in the medium, so the time for an echo to return is directly proportional to the distance. The precision of the echo time sets the smallest difference in distance you can resolve.

concepts.name: Sound intensity
concepts.statement: Intensity is the power per unit area carried by a wave, where power is the rate at which the wave transfers energy, and its SI unit is the watt per metre squared. It is the physical quantity behind loudness, and it applies to every sound, audible or not. The intensities of ordinary sounds are small: only about 10⁻¹⁶ W falls on the eardrum at the threshold of hearing.

concepts.name: Intensity and pressure amplitude
concepts.statement: The intensity of a sound wave is proportional to its amplitude squared. The pressure amplitude is half the difference between the maximum and minimum pressure in the wave, the density is that of the material the sound travels in, and the speed is the speed of sound in that medium. The energy of an oscillating element of air is proportional to its amplitude squared, and the pressure variation is proportional to the amplitude of the oscillation. The intensity therefore goes as the square of the pressure amplitude: the greater the amplitude, the more the sound compresses the air.

concepts.name: Sound intensity level
concepts.statement: We quote sound intensity levels in decibels much more often than intensities in watts per metre squared, because the logarithm of the intensity describes how our ears perceive sound better than the intensity itself. The level of a sound of intensity $I$ is ten times the logarithm of its ratio to the reference intensity $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m². Because it is a ratio, the level is unitless and gives the sound relative to a fixed standard. The "deci" in decibel says that the ratio's logarithm is multiplied by ten.

forms.condition: I₀ = 10⁻¹² W/m²

concepts.name: Threshold of hearing
concepts.statement: The reference intensity $I_0 = 10^{-12}$ W/m² is the lowest intensity of sound a person with normal hearing can perceive at a frequency of 1000 Hz, and its level is 0 dB because the logarithm of one is zero. The ear is sensitive to as little as a trillionth of a watt per metre squared, when the air molecules vibrate over less than one molecular diameter and the gauge pressures are less than 10⁻⁹ atm, and it tolerates sounds 10¹² times as intense; a range that wide is why the logarithmic scale fits experience better than the intensities themselves.

concepts.name: Intensity ratios in decibels
concepts.statement: Each factor of 10 in intensity corresponds to 10 dB, so a 90 dB sound is three factors of 10, or 1000 times, as intense as a 60 dB sound. Because the logarithm of a ratio is the difference of the logarithms, the difference in level between two sounds depends only on the ratio of their intensities: doubling the intensity raises the level by about 3 dB and a factor of five raises it by 7 dB, whatever the intensities themselves are.

concepts.name: Adding the intensities of sources
concepts.statement: When many sources sound together and interference can be neglected, their intensities add, and the level rises by ten times the logarithm of how many there are: a thousand flies at 40.0 dB each make 70.0 dB, and ten stereos making 120 dB at the centre of a circle each contribute 110 dB. The rule is the decibel relation applied to a ratio that is a count.

concepts.name: Sound pressure level
concepts.statement: Another decibel scale, the sound pressure level, uses the ratio of the pressure amplitude to a reference pressure rather than of intensity to a reference intensity. It is common where sound travels in water, and it can give very different decibel numbers for the same sound. Ocean noise from ships may be 200 dB as a sound pressure level where the sound intensity level would be under 140 dB. Its numbers run 60 to 70 dB above the levels this text uses, as 17.7 notes.

concepts.name: Doppler effect
concepts.statement: The Doppler effect is an alteration in the observed frequency of a sound due to motion of either the source or the observer, and the actual change in frequency is the Doppler shift. Each compression spreads out spherically from the point where the source emitted it. When the source moves, the point of emission moves, so the compressions are closer together ahead of the source and farther apart behind it. The medium fixes the speed of sound, so a shorter wavelength arrives as a higher frequency. When the observer moves instead, the rate at which she meets the compressions changes. Relative motion toward one another raises the received frequency, motion apart lowers it, and the greater the relative speed, the greater the effect.

concepts.name: Doppler shift for a moving source
concepts.statement: For a stationary observer and a moving source, the frequency received is the source frequency times the ratio of the speed of sound to the speed of sound plus or minus the source's speed along the line joining them, the minus sign for motion toward the observer and the plus sign for motion away. The greater the speed of the source, the greater the effect, and the shifts toward and away are not symmetric.

forms.condition: stationary observer, moving source; minus for motion toward the observer, plus for motion away

concepts.name: Doppler shift for a moving observer
concepts.statement: For a stationary source and a moving observer, the received frequency is the source frequency times the ratio of the speed of sound plus or minus the observer's speed to the speed of sound. The plus sign is for motion toward the source and the minus sign for motion away. The form differs from the moving-source case because the observer passes through more or fewer crests of a wave whose wavelength stays the same.

forms.condition: stationary source, moving observer; plus for motion toward the source, minus for motion away

concepts.name: Doppler shift for source and observer moving
concepts.statement: When both move relative to the air there are two Doppler shifts, one for the moving observer and one for the moving source, and the received frequency is the product of the two factors. Source and observer carried together, as an engineer and the horn of the same train, receive the emitted frequency unchanged because the factors cancel; what matters is that they are not moving relative to each other.

forms.condition: both source and observer moving

concepts.name: Sonic booms
concepts.statement: As a source's speed approaches the speed of sound, the observed frequency ahead of it approaches infinity, because each successive wave piles onto the previous one. If the source exceeds the speed of sound, no sound reaches an observer until the source has passed. The waves interfere constructively along the lines of a cone, and this superposition is a sonic boom, a constructive interference of sound created by an object moving faster than sound. Inside the cone the interference is mostly destructive. The faster the source, the smaller the cone's angle. An aircraft makes two booms, one from its nose and one from its tail.

concepts.name: Bow wakes
concepts.statement: Sonic booms are one example of a bow wake, the V-shaped disturbance created when a wave source moves faster than the wave propagation speed. Water waves spread in circles from the point where they are made, and a duck moving faster than they spread leaves the familiar wake; a subatomic particle moving through water faster than light moves in water leaves a cone of light called Cerenkov radiation.

concepts.name: Doppler shift
concepts.statement: The Doppler shift is the actual change in frequency due to relative motion of source and observer.

concepts.name: Sound interference
concepts.statement: Interference is the hallmark of waves, and one way to prove something is a wave is to observe interference effects. Sound waves in fluids are pressure waves consistent with Pascal's principle, so pressures from two sources add and subtract like simple numbers: positive and negative gauge pressures add to a much smaller pressure and a lower-intensity sound. Noise-cancelling headphones introduce a second sound with its maxima and minima exactly reversed from the incoming noise, and the beats from two similar notes played together are interference too.

concepts.name: Resonance of an air column
concepts.statement: An air column has only certain natural frequencies. A disturbance from a tuning fork travels down a tube at the speed of sound and bounces off the closed end. If the tube is just the right length, the reflected sound arrives back at the fork exactly half a cycle later and interferes constructively with the continuing sound. The incoming and reflected sounds then form a standing wave. Only the resonant frequencies interfere constructively to form standing waves, while others interfere destructively and are absent. Every sound resonance, from a bottle's toot to a singer's voice, is a matter of interference. Think of it as a natural vibration of the air column, whatever starts it.

concepts.name: Nodes and antinodes in a tube
concepts.statement: In a tube closed at one end, the standing wave has its maximum air displacement, an antinode, at the open end, where the air moves freely. It has no displacement, a node, at the closed end, where the air cannot move. The distance from a node to an antinode is one-fourth of a wavelength, so for the lowest resonance the wavelength is four times the tube's length. A tube open at both ends has antinodes at both ends and half a wavelength inside for its lowest resonance.

concepts.name: Fundamental, overtones and harmonics
concepts.statement: The lowest resonant frequency of a system is its fundamental, and all higher resonant frequencies are overtones. Every resonant frequency is an integral multiple of the fundamental, so together they are called harmonics: the fundamental is the first harmonic, the first overtone the second harmonic, and so on. For a tube closed at one end the first overtone is three times the fundamental and so is the third harmonic. Which overtones are present, and how intense they are, makes a trumpet's middle C differ from a clarinet's and one voice from another.

concepts.name: Resonances of a closed tube
concepts.statement: With one-fourth of a wavelength in the tube at the fundamental and three-fourths at the first overtone, the pattern generalises to a single expression: the resonant frequencies of a tube closed at one end are odd multiples of the speed of sound over four times the length. They depend on the speed of sound and hence on temperature, which is why musicians bring their wind instruments to room temperature before playing them together.

forms.condition: tube closed at one end
tube closed at one end, λ = 4L
tube closed at one end, λ′ = 4L/3

concepts.name: Resonances of an open tube
concepts.statement: A tube open at both ends has maximum air displacements at both ends, so its resonant frequencies are all integer multiples of the speed of sound over twice the length. Its fundamental is twice that of the same tube closed at one end, and it has a different spectrum of overtones. Two tubes with the same fundamental, one open and one closed, therefore sound different when played.

forms.condition: tube open at both ends

concepts.name: Finding a tube’s length or frequency
concepts.statement: To find the length of a tube that sounds a given fundamental, or the frequency a given length sounds, first find the speed of sound on the day from the air temperature. Then solve the resonance relation for the tube's kind of ends for the unknown. The same reckoning gives the range of fundamentals of the ear canal and the fraction by which an instrument's frequencies change between a cold and a warm room.

forms.condition: tube closed at one end

concepts.name: Resonance in musical instruments
concepts.statement: Wind instruments use resonance in air columns to amplify tones made by lips or reeds, and string instruments use sounding boxes: the vibrating string creates a sound that resonates in the box, greatly amplifying it and creating overtones that give the instrument its characteristic flavour, the more complex the box's shape the wider the range of frequencies it can resonate over. A marimba's gourds and a violin's body do the same work, and so does the cavity of the throat and mouth in speech. The ideas apply to any system with wave characteristics, down to the standing waves of an atom's electrons.

concepts.name: Antinode
concepts.statement: An antinode is a point of maximum displacement in a standing wave. In a tube it lies at an open end, where the air moves freely.

concepts.name: Node
concepts.statement: A node is a point of zero displacement in a standing wave. In a tube it lies at a closed end, where the air cannot move.

concepts.name: Fundamental
concepts.statement: The fundamental is the lowest-frequency resonance of a system.

concepts.name: Overtones
concepts.statement: Overtones are all the resonant frequencies of a system higher than the fundamental.

concepts.name: Harmonics
concepts.statement: Harmonics is the term used to refer collectively to the fundamental and its overtones, each an integral multiple of the fundamental. The fundamental is the first harmonic.

concepts.name: Audible range
concepts.statement: Normal human hearing encompasses frequencies from 20 to 20,000 Hz. Sounds below 20 Hz are infrasound and those above 20,000 Hz are ultrasound; neither is perceived by the ear, though infrasound can sometimes be felt as vibrations. Other animals hear differently: dogs to 30,000 Hz, bats and dolphins to 100,000 Hz, elephants below 20 Hz.

concepts.name: How finely pitch is discriminated
concepts.statement: Most of us have excellent relative pitch and can tell whether one sound has a different frequency from another when the frequencies differ by 0.3% or more, so that 500.0 and 501.5 Hz are noticeably different. Pitch perception is directly related to frequency and is not greatly affected by intensity. Musical notes are particular sounds with particular names, and the uncommon ability to name one on hearing it is perfect pitch.

concepts.name: Loudness
concepts.statement: The perception of intensity is loudness. At a given frequency you can discern a difference of about 1 dB and easily notice a change of 3 dB. Loudness does not depend on intensity alone. The ear is most sensitive between 2000 and 5000 Hz, so sounds there seem louder than sounds of the same intensity at 500 or 10,000 Hz, and sounds near the extremes of the hearing range seem less loud still. The ear responds over a range of a trillion in intensity, which very few instruments can match.

concepts.name: Timbre
concepts.statement: When a violin and a piano play the same middle C there is no mistaking one for the other, because each produces a distinctive set of frequencies and intensities. Our perception of these combinations is tone quality, or timbre, described by words such as dull, brilliant, warm or rich; it is more subjective than loudness or pitch and takes the subject into perceptual psychology. A note is the basic unit of music with a specific name, and combinations of notes constitute music.

concepts.name: Reading equal-loudness curves
concepts.statement: A phon is the unit of loudness perception, as the decibel is the unit of physical intensity level, and the two are numerically equal at 1000 Hz. The equal-loudness curves relate loudness to intensity level and frequency for persons with normal hearing. Every sound along a given curve sounds equally loud. To find a sound's loudness, locate its frequency and intensity level on the grid and interpolate between the curves. To find the level a sound needs for a given loudness, follow that curve to the frequency. The curves dip between 2000 and 5000 Hz, where the ear is most sensitive, and rise at both extremes. Sounds below the 0-phon curve are not heard, and a few sounds below 0 dB are.

concepts.name: Hearing loss and audiograms
concepts.statement: Most conversational sound falls in a band of frequencies and intensity levels. With a hearing loss of 40 phons at all frequencies, you can still understand conversation, though quietly. A 60-phon loss leaves only the lowest frequencies, and you cannot understand speech unless it is much louder than normal. Hearing tests run from 250 to 8000 Hz and appear as an audiogram, whose threshold is relative to the normal threshold, so normal hearing registers as 0 dB at every frequency. Loss caused by noise shows a dip near 4000 Hz, whatever frequency caused it. The most common loss, presbycusis, comes with age and is increasingly severe at higher frequencies.

concepts.name: Hearing mechanism
concepts.statement: The ear is a transducer that converts sound waves into electrical nerve impulses. The outer ear, or ear canal, carries sound to the eardrum and resonates as an air column, which is partly why the ear is most sensitive between 2000 and 5000 Hz. The middle ear's lever system takes the force the sound pressure exerts on the eardrum, amplifies it and applies it through the oval window to the much smaller area of the cochlea. The pressure waves there are about 40 times greater than those on the eardrum. Two muscles react to intense sound in a few milliseconds and reduce the force transmitted. In the inner ear the pressure waves make the tectorial membrane vibrate against the hair cells. These resonate at different positions for different frequencies, high near the base and low at the far end. Below about 1000 Hz the nerves signal at the sound's own frequency, and above it by position. Sound can reach the cochlea through the skull when conduction fails, and a cochlear implant can stand in for lost cilia by stimulating the nerves directly.

concepts.name: Phon
concepts.statement: The phon is the numerical unit of loudness. A sound's loudness in phons is the intensity level in decibels of a 1000 Hz tone that sounds equally loud, so at 1000 Hz phons and decibels are numerically equal.

concepts.name: Note
concepts.statement: A note is a basic unit of music with a specific name, such as middle C, and notes are combined to make tunes.

concepts.name: Ultrasound
concepts.statement: Ultrasound is sound with frequencies above 20,000 Hz, the top of the range of normal human hearing. The ear does not perceive it.

concepts.name: Infrasound
concepts.statement: Infrasound is sound with frequencies below 20 Hz, the bottom of the range of normal human hearing. The ear does not perceive it, though it can sometimes be felt as vibrations.

concepts.name: Ultrasound as probe and treatment
concepts.statement: Ultrasound is any sound above 20 kHz, and its characteristics, frequency, intensity and a wavelength that limits the detail it can detect, are wave properties common to all waves. Like any wave it carries energy that the medium absorbs, with effects that vary with intensity: focused to 10³ to 10⁵ W/m² it shatters gallstones and pulverises tissue, partly through cavitation, the creation and collapse of vapour cavities; at 10³ to 10⁴ W/m² it is the deep heating of ultrasound diathermy; diagnostic intensities of about 10⁻² W/m² are too low to do thermal damage, and decades of use show no ill effects.

concepts.name: Acoustic impedance
concepts.statement: Reflections at boundaries between two media occur because of differences in their acoustic impedance, the product of a medium's density and the speed of sound through it, in kg/(m²·s). The acoustic impedances of soft tissues do not vary much, but there is a big difference between soft tissue and air and between soft tissue and bone, which is why those boundaries reflect so strongly.

concepts.name: Intensity reflection coefficient
concepts.statement: At a boundary between media of different acoustic impedance, part of the wave energy reflects and part passes through, and the greater the difference in impedance, the greater the reflection. The intensity reflection coefficient is the ratio of the reflected intensity to the incident intensity. It is zero, total transmission, when the two impedances are the same, and an impedance match couples sound efficiently from one medium into another. An ultrasound image tracks these reflections and maps their intensity in a plane.

concepts.name: Resolution and penetration of ultrasound
concepts.statement: A transducer, a piezoelectric crystal, both sends the ultrasound and records its echoes, and the time between the signal and each echo gives the depth of each boundary at the speed of sound in tissue, about 1540 m/s. It is very difficult to detect details smaller than the wavelength of a probe: at 7 MHz the wavelength in tissue is 0.22 mm, and in practice 1 mm detail is attainable. Higher frequencies give finer detail but penetrate less, the rule of thumb being a useful depth of about 500 wavelengths, so they suit small organs such as the eye and not the deep abdomen.

concepts.name: Doppler-shifted ultrasound
concepts.statement: Ultrasound reflected from moving blood or a beating fetal heart is Doppler shifted twice. The reflector receives a shifted frequency as a moving observer and then returns it as a moving source, and the magnitude of the shift is directly proportional to the reflector's velocity. The echo adds to the broadcast frequency to produce beats, whose frequency is the absolute difference of the two. The shift itself, a few hundred hertz out of a couple of megahertz, is hard to measure. The beat frequency is easy to measure, ignores any drift in the broadcast frequency and falls in the audible range. Doppler radar measures wind, aircraft and car speeds by the same principle.

concepts.name: Electric potential energy
concepts.statement: The electrostatic or Coulomb force is conservative, which means that the work done on a charge is independent of the path taken, exactly as for gravity in the absence of friction. When a force is conservative, it is possible to define a potential energy associated with the force, and it is usually easier to deal with the potential energy, because it depends only on position, than to calculate the work directly. The work done by a conservative force is the negative of the change in potential energy, so work done to accelerate a positive charge from rest is positive and results from a loss in PE.

concepts.name: Electric potential
concepts.statement: The electric potential is the potential energy per unit charge, $V = \text{PE}/q$. Since the work done by the field, and hence the change in potential energy, is proportional to the test charge, the dependence on the charge cancels and $V$ does not depend on $q$.

concepts.name: Potential difference
concepts.statement: The potential difference between points A and B is the change in potential energy of a charge moved from A to B, divided by the charge. Its unit, the joule per coulomb, is the volt, named after Alessandro Volta. Voltage is the common name for potential difference, and a voltage always means the potential difference between two points. Voltage is not the same as energy: a motorcycle battery and a car battery can both be 12 V, yet one stores much more energy than the other.

concepts.name: Finding energy from a potential difference
concepts.statement: The relationship between potential difference and electrical potential energy can be read either way: the potential difference is the change in potential energy per unit charge, and the change in potential energy is the charge times the potential difference. To find the energy a battery delivers, multiply the charge it moves by its voltage; to find the charge that moved, divide the energy by the voltage. The energies so found are absolute values, and the change in potential energy of a battery that loses energy is negative.

concepts.name: Charge motion and potential
concepts.statement: Downhill for the electron is uphill for a positive charge. A battery repels electrons from its negative terminal and attracts them to its positive terminal, so the negative charge moves from A to B through a change in potential of +12 V, and since the charge is negative, $\Delta\text{PE} = q\Delta V$ is negative and the potential energy of the battery has decreased. In terms of potential, the positive terminal is at a higher voltage than the negative, whichever sign of charge moves.

concepts.name: Zero of potential
concepts.statement: The point you choose to be zero volts is arbitrary, exactly as gravitational potential energy has an arbitrary zero such as sea level or a lecture hall floor. Every battery has two terminals, and its voltage is the potential difference between them; a potential quoted for a single point assumes a reference, usually infinity for a point charge or the ground for a meter, and it is the potential difference between two points that is of importance.

concepts.name: Electron volt
concepts.statement: On the submicroscopic scale the energy per particle is a tiny fraction of a joule, yet it can be enough to break up organic molecules and harm living tissue, so an energy unit on that scale is convenient. The electron volt is the energy a fundamental charge gains when accelerated through a potential difference of 1 V. An electron accelerated through 50 V gains 50 eV, and a doubly charged ion accelerated through 100 V gains 200 eV. The energy of the electron in electron volts is numerically the same as the voltage between the plates.

concepts.name: Conservation of energy for a charge
concepts.statement: The total energy of a system stays constant if no work or heat transfer adds to it or takes from it. For conservative forces such as the electrostatic force, conservation of energy says that mechanical energy, the sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy, is a constant. A loss of PE of a charged particle becomes an increase in its KE, where PE is now the electric potential energy. As many times before, energy gives insight and makes problems easier than following the force.

forms.condition: conservative forces only
conservative forces only

concepts.name: Finding the speed of an accelerated charge
concepts.statement: With only conservative forces acting, all of the electrical potential energy of a charge accelerated from rest in a vacuum becomes kinetic energy, so $qV = mv^2/2$ gives the final speed. The large final speed of an electron confirms that the gravitational force is negligible. It also shows how easily small voltages accelerate electrons, because of their very small mass. Voltages much higher than 100 V produce speeds so great that relativistic effects matter.

forms.condition: a charge accelerated from rest, non-relativistic

concepts.name: Voltage and field between parallel plates
concepts.statement: In a uniform electric field the voltage between two points is the field strength times the distance between them along the field, $V_\text{AB} = Ed$, so the field is the voltage divided by the distance. The work the field does on a positive charge moved from the positive plate to the negative plate is both $qV_\text{AB}$ and $qEd$, and the charge cancels.

forms.condition: uniform electric field only

concepts.name: Potential as scalar, field as vector
concepts.statement: Either the potential difference or the electric field can describe any charge distribution. The potential difference is most closely tied to energy and is a scalar quantity with no direction, whereas the field is most closely related to force and is a vector with both magnitude and direction. The distinction matters when several charges act: voltages add as numbers, whereas fields add as vectors.

concepts.name: Units of the electric field
concepts.statement: The relation $E = V_\text{AB}/d$ implies that the units for electric field are volts per meter, and the units already known from the definition of the field are newtons per coulomb, so the two must be the same unit. Which of the two is written depends on whether the field is being read from a force or from a voltage; the force on a charge in Example 19.5 comes out in newtons because 1 V/m is 1 N/C.

concepts.name: Dielectric breakdown of air
concepts.statement: Dry air will support a maximum electric field strength of about $3.0 \times 10^6$ V/m. Above that value the field ionizes enough of the air to make it a conductor, allowing a discharge or spark that reduces the field. It therefore takes about 75 kV to make a spark jump across a 2.5 cm gap, which limits the voltages that can exist between conductors, such as those on a power transmission line. Points on a surface create greater fields than smooth surfaces and so spark at a smaller voltage, and humid air breaks down at a lower field strength than dry.

concepts.name: Field as potential gradient
concepts.statement: In general, whether or not the electric field is uniform, it points in the direction of decreasing potential, because the force on a positive charge points both along the field and toward lower potential. The magnitude of the field equals the rate of decrease of the potential with distance: the faster the potential decreases over distance, the greater the field. The minus sign says that the field points toward decreasing potential. For continually changing potentials the differences become infinitesimals, and you need differential calculus.

concepts.name: Electric potential of a point charge
concepts.statement: Point charges such as electrons are among the fundamental building blocks of matter, and spherical charge distributions create external fields exactly like a point charge, so the potential of a point charge is essential. Calculus gives the work needed to move a test charge from a large distance away to a distance $r$ from a point charge. With $W = -q\Delta V$, it shows that the potential is $kQ/r$, with zero potential at infinity. A negative value means the charge attracts a positive charge from a larger distance, since the potential there is lower than at larger distances.

forms.condition: point charge, with V = 0 at infinity

concepts.name: Potential versus field of a point charge
concepts.statement: The potential of a point charge decreases with distance, whereas the field of a point charge decreases with distance squared, since the field is the force per unit charge and Coulomb's law is an inverse square law. The two describe the same charge in two ways, and the difference in their fall-off is the difference between an energy per charge, which accumulates over the whole path in from infinity, and a force per charge, which acts at one point.

concepts.name: Superposition of potentials
concepts.statement: To find the voltage due to a combination of point charges, add the individual voltages as numbers. To find the total electric field, add the individual fields as vectors, taking magnitude and direction into account. This fits the fact that the potential goes with energy, a scalar, whereas the field goes with force, a vector. It makes the potential the easier quantity to work with when several charges are present.

concepts.name: Potential outside a charged sphere
concepts.statement: Charge on a metal sphere spreads out uniformly and produces a field like that of a point charge at its center. The potential on the surface and outside the sphere is therefore that of an equal point charge at the center, and you read the potential near the surface at the sphere's radius. That is why a Van de Graaff terminal's charge and radius set its voltage, and why isolated charge is difficult to store: a relatively small charge produces a large voltage.

concepts.name: Finding the potential energy of two charges
concepts.statement: To find the potential energy of a pair of point charges, take the potential of one at the position of the other and multiply by the second charge, since the potential is the potential energy per unit charge. The energy of a system of several charges is the sum over every pair. It is negative for unlike charges, which attract, and positive for like charges, which repel. Bringing like charges closer raises it, and bringing unlike charges closer lowers it.

concepts.name: Equipotential lines and equipotential surfaces
concepts.statement: You can picture electric potentials, just as field lines picture electric fields. Lines along which the electric potential is constant are equipotential lines in two dimensions, or equipotential surfaces in three, and equipotential also serves as a noun. The potential of a point charge, $kQ/r$, is the same anywhere on a sphere of radius $r$ surrounding the charge. An equipotential surface of a point charge is therefore a sphere and, in the plane, a circle. Moving a charge anywhere along one of these lines takes no work, and moving a charge from one equipotential to another takes work.

concepts.name: Equipotentials perpendicular to field lines
concepts.statement: Moving a charge along an equipotential takes no work, since the potential difference along it is zero, and work is zero only if the force is perpendicular to the motion. The force on a charge is in the direction of the field, so motion along an equipotential must be perpendicular to the field. With neither the charge, the field nor the distance zero, the cosine of the angle between them must vanish and the angle must be 90°. The rule holds in every case, and it lets you draw the equipotential lines from the field lines and the field lines from the equipotentials.

forms.condition: motion along an equipotential
motion along an equipotential

concepts.name: Conductor as an equipotential
concepts.statement: The electric field must be perpendicular to the surface of any conductor in static situations, and equipotentials are perpendicular to the field, so a conductor is an equipotential surface. There can be no voltage difference across the surface of a conductor, or charges would flow. Because a conductor is an equipotential, it can replace any equipotential surface. A charged spherical conductor can replace the point charge at the center of its equipotential spheres and leave the field and the potential outside unchanged. Conducting plates placed at the equipotential lines between two plates would maintain the same field.

concepts.name: Drawing equipotential lines
concepts.statement: Given the electric field lines, draw the equipotential lines perpendicular to them. Given the equipotential lines, as a voltmeter might measure them in a laboratory, draw the field lines perpendicular to the equipotentials. The potential is greatest near a positive charge and least near a negative one, so you can mark the direction of increasing potential too, and the field lines point from higher to lower potential.

concepts.name: Equipotential spacing and field strength
concepts.statement: Between two parallel conducting plates the equipotentials are evenly spaced and parallel, because the field is uniform and the potential falls at a constant rate across the gap. Where the field is stronger the potential changes faster with distance, so equipotentials drawn at equal steps of voltage crowd together; where it is weaker they spread apart. As the isolines of potential get closer together the field gets stronger, as a hill is steeper where the contours of gravitational potential crowd.

concepts.name: Capacitor
concepts.statement: A capacitor is a device that stores electric charge, with applications ranging from filtering static out of radio reception to energy storage in heart defibrillators. A commercial capacitor typically has two conducting parts close to one another but not touching, usually with an insulator between them. When you connect battery terminals to an initially uncharged capacitor, equal amounts of positive and negative charge separate onto its two plates. The capacitor remains neutral overall, but it is said to store a charge $Q$. The amount of charge it can store depends on the voltage applied and on its physical characteristics, such as its size.

concepts.name: Capacitance
concepts.statement: Capacitance is the amount of charge a capacitor stores per volt applied across it, $C = Q/V$. The greater the voltage applied to any capacitor, the greater the charge stored in it, and different capacitors store different charges for the same voltage. The unit of capacitance, the farad, is a coulomb per volt, a very large capacitance, and typical capacitors run from picofarads to millifarads.

forms.latex: E \propto Q, \quad V \propto E, \quad Q \propto V

concepts.name: Capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor
concepts.statement: A parallel plate capacitor is two identical conducting plates of area $A$ separated by a distance $d$. Like charges repel, unlike charges attract and the force between charges decreases with distance. The bigger the plates, the more charge they can store, because the charges can spread out more. The closer the plates, the greater the attraction of the opposite charges on them. The capacitance therefore grows with the area and shrinks with the separation, and these are the only two factors. The constant is the permittivity of free space, $8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ F/m, whose small value goes with the large size of the farad: a parallel plate capacitor must have a large area to approach a farad.

forms.condition: parallel plates separated by air or free space

concepts.name: Dielectric
concepts.statement: Making the separation smaller gives a larger capacitance, but then the maximum voltage must drop in proportion to avoid breakdown, since $E = V/d$. An important solution is to put an insulating material, called a dielectric, between the plates and make the separation as small as possible. The smaller separation raises the capacitance, and many insulators also withstand greater electric fields than air before breaking down. Water has a large dielectric constant but rarely serves as one, and humid air sparks at a lower voltage than dry.

concepts.name: Capacitance with a dielectric
concepts.statement: With a dielectric between the plates, the capacitance is greater than that of the same plates in vacuum by a factor $\kappa$, called the dielectric constant, which depends on the material. The constant for vacuum is exactly 1 and for air very close to it. Air-filled capacitors therefore act much like those with vacuum between their plates, except that air can become conductive if the field grows too great. Teflon's constant is 2.1, water's 80 and strontium titanate's 233. The same capacitor filled with Teflon has a greater capacitance and takes a much greater voltage, and so stores 42 times the charge.

forms.condition: parallel plate capacitor with dielectric

concepts.name: Dielectric strength
concepts.statement: The dielectric strength of an insulating material is the maximum electric field strength above which it begins to break down and conduct. The field between parallel plates is the voltage over the separation, so the dielectric strength limits the voltage you can apply for a given plate separation. For 1.00 mm of air the limit is 3000 V, and for 1.00 mm of Teflon, whose strength is $60 \times 10^6$ V/m, it is 60,000 V.

concepts.name: Polarization of a dielectric
concepts.statement: Microscopically, a dielectric increases capacitance because it polarizes: the more easily its molecules polarize, the greater its dielectric constant. The Coulomb force between the closest ends of the polarized molecules and the charge on the plates is attractive and very strong, since they are very close together. It attracts more charge onto the plates than if the space were empty. Seen the other way, the field lines end on the surface charges of the dielectric, so fewer of them cross from one plate to the other. The field inside is less than in vacuum for the same charge, and so is the voltage $V = Ed$, and since $C = Q/V$ the capacitance is greater. The dielectric constant is the ratio of the field in vacuum to the field in the material, and it depends closely on the polarizability of the material. An atom polarizes because the external charges shift its electron cloud, and a polar molecule such as water carries an inherent separation of charge and so polarizes more readily.

concepts.name: Permittivity of free space
concepts.statement: The permittivity of free space is the constant $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12}$ F/m that sets the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a vacuum between its plates. Its small value is related to the large size of the farad.

concepts.name: Parallel plate capacitor
concepts.statement: A parallel plate capacitor is two identical conducting plates separated by a distance.

concepts.name: Equivalent capacitance
concepts.statement: Many applications connect several capacitors together, and the combination acts like a single equivalent capacitor. Its total capacitance depends both on the individual capacitors and on how they are connected. Two simple and common types of connection, series and parallel, give totals that are easy to calculate, and some more complicated connections reduce to combinations of the two.

concepts.name: Capacitance in series
concepts.statement: When you apply a voltage across a series connection of capacitors, opposite charges of magnitude $Q$ flow to either side of the originally uncharged combination. Conservation of charge requires equal-magnitude charges on the plates of each individual capacitor, since these originally neutral devices only separate charge. The voltages across the individual capacitors are $Q/C_1$, $Q/C_2$ and $Q/C_3$, and the total voltage is their sum. Writing the total as $Q/C_\text{S}$ and cancelling the charge gives the sum of reciprocals. The combination resembles a single capacitor with a larger effective plate separation than any of the individual ones, so the total capacitance in series is less than any of the individual capacitances.

forms.condition: capacitors in series
capacitors in series

concepts.name: Capacitance in parallel
concepts.statement: In a parallel connection the voltage across each capacitor equals that of the source, since a conductor connects each one directly to it and conductors are equipotentials. Each capacitor therefore holds the charge it would hold alone. The total charge is the sum of the individual charges, $C_\text{p}V = C_1V + C_2V + C_3V$, and cancelling the voltage makes the total capacitance in parallel simply the sum of the individual capacitances. The equivalent capacitor has an effectively larger plate area and so a larger capacitance.

forms.condition: capacitors in parallel
capacitors in parallel

concepts.name: Reducing series and parallel capacitors
concepts.statement: More complicated connections of capacitors can sometimes be combinations of series and parallel. To find the total capacitance, identify the series and parallel parts, compute their capacitances, and then find the total. For example, replace two capacitors in series by their series capacitance, then add it in parallel to a third. Working piece by piece until you reach a total works for larger combinations too.

concepts.name: Energy stored in a capacitor
concepts.statement: Energy stored in a capacitor is electrical potential energy and depends on the charge and voltage on the capacitor. Apply $\Delta\text{PE} = q\Delta V$ with care, because the capacitor starts with zero voltage and comes up to its full voltage as it charges. The average voltage during charging is half the final voltage, so the energy stored is half the product of the charge and the voltage, not the whole product. Since $Q = CV$, you can write the same energy in terms of any two of the charge, the voltage and the capacitance. The energy is in joules for a charge in coulombs, a voltage in volts and a capacitance in farads.

concepts.name: Average voltage while charging
concepts.statement: The first charge placed on a capacitor experiences a change in voltage of zero, since the capacitor has zero voltage when uncharged, and the final charge experiences the full voltage, since the capacitor now has its full voltage on it. The voltage rises in proportion to the charge, so the average voltage on the capacitor during the charging process is half the final voltage, and that is the voltage the full charge is to be taken as having passed through. This is why the energy is $QV/2$ and not $QV$.

concepts.name: Uses of capacitor energy
concepts.statement: A defibrillator stores its energy in a capacitor, and the operator can adjust it to fit the situation. A large charge delivered in a short burst to a set of paddles across a person's chest can stop the fast, irregular beating of cardiac or ventricular fibrillation and let the body's pacemaker resume normal patterns. Automated external defibrillators in many public places diagnose the patient's heart condition and apply the shock with appropriate energy and waveform. Less dramatically, capacitors in microelectronics supply energy while you change batteries, and they power the flash lamps on cameras.

concepts.name: Defibrillator
concepts.statement: A defibrillator is a machine that delivers an electrical shock to a heart attack victim's heart to restore its normal beating pattern. It stores its energy in a capacitor and releases it in a burst.

concepts.name: Electric current
concepts.statement: Electric current is the rate at which charge flows. A large current, such as the one that starts a truck engine, moves a large amount of charge in a small time, while a small current, such as the one that runs a handheld calculator, moves a small amount of charge over a long time. Because current is a rate rather than an amount, the same idea describes a lightning bolt and a clock battery, and every other result in the chapter builds on it.

concepts.name: Ampere
concepts.statement: Since current is a charge divided by a time, its SI unit is one coulomb per second, named the ampere for the French physicist André-Marie Ampère. Fuses, circuit breakers and many electrical appliances carry ratings in amperes.

concepts.name: Conventional current
concepts.statement: The direction of conventional current is the direction that positive charge would flow. Depending on the situation, positive charges, negative charges, or both may move. In metal wires electrons carry the current, in ionic solutions such as salt water both signs move, and a Van de Graaff generator can produce a current of pure positive charges. One convention lets the same circuit analysis apply whatever the carriers are. Keep in mind that the electrons in a wire actually move opposite to the current drawn on the diagram.

concepts.name: Reading a circuit schematic
concepts.statement: A schematic represents a battery by two parallel lines, a conducting wire by a straight line and a load by a zigzag. A single schematic can stand for anything from a truck battery lighting a headlight to a small battery lighting a keyhole. Because the analysis is the same for a wide variety of situations, understanding a few schematics lets you apply the concepts to many more.

concepts.name: Charge carriers
concepts.statement: Current is the flow of free charges, and which charges are free depends on the material. In a metal the free charges are electrons far enough from their nuclei to move among the atoms in a sea, while in an ionic solution or a nerve cell ions of both signs move. A conductor carrying a current has an electric field in it, which supplies the energy to move the charges. It is therefore not in static equilibrium, as the conductors of the previous two chapters were.

concepts.name: Drift velocity
concepts.statement: The drift velocity is the average velocity of the free charges in a conductor. An individual electron moves quickly and almost at random, colliding with atoms and with other electrons, but an electric field tilts that random walk so that the whole crowd creeps one way. The drift velocity is quite small, on the order of $10^{-4}$ m/s, because there are so many free charges: the larger the density of carriers, the lower the velocity needed to carry a given current.

concepts.name: Signal speed versus drift
concepts.statement: Electrical signals travel at speeds on the order of $10^{8}$ m/s, about $10^{12}$ times the drift velocity of the charges that carry them. The force between charges acts rapidly at a distance, and that reconciles the two speeds. A charge forced into one end of a wire pushes the charges ahead of it, which push on charges farther down the line. The signal is a rapidly propagating change in electric field, not the arrival of any particular electron.

concepts.name: Current and drift velocity
concepts.statement: Counting the free charges in a segment of wire gives the current directly. A segment of cross-sectional area $A$ and length $x$ holds $nAx$ carriers of charge $q$ each, and if they all leave the segment in a time $\Delta t$, the current is that charge divided by that time. Since $x/\Delta t$ is the drift velocity, the current is $I = nqAv_\text{d}$. This ties the number you measure with an ammeter to the microscopic picture of a crowd of electrons.

concepts.name: Ohm’s law
concepts.statement: Georg Simon Ohm was the first to demonstrate experimentally that the current in a metal wire is directly proportional to the voltage applied to it. Combining that proportionality with the fact that current is inversely proportional to resistance gives $I = V/R$, which can be read as a cause-and-effect relationship with voltage the cause and current the effect. It is the relation the rest of the chapter, and the whole of circuit analysis, rests on.

concepts.name: Resistance
concepts.statement: If voltage drives current, something must impede it, and that electric property is called resistance. Collisions of moving charges with the atoms and molecules of a substance transfer energy to the substance and limit the current, so current is inversely proportional to resistance and is cut in half if the resistance doubles. Resistances range over many orders of magnitude, from $10^{-5}\;\Omega$ for a meter of thick copper wire to $10^{12}\;\Omega$ for a ceramic insulator.

concepts.name: Ohm
concepts.statement: The unit of resistance is one volt per ampere, which is named the ohm and written with the capital Greek omega, $1\;\Omega = 1\;\text{V/A}$. An object that has simple resistance is called a resistor, even when its resistance is small.

concepts.name: Ohmic materials
concepts.statement: Ohm's law, like Hooke's law, is not universally valid. The many substances that obey it are called ohmic, and they include good conductors like copper and aluminum and some poor conductors under certain circumstances. An ohmic material has a resistance that does not depend on the voltage across it or the current through it. Because the law is empirical rather than fundamental, you need to know when a straight line through the origin is the right model and when it is not.

concepts.name: Simple circuit
concepts.statement: A simple circuit has a single voltage source and a single resistor, with the connecting wires assumed to have negligible resistance or their resistance included in $R$. It is the smallest complete circuit there is, and settling how voltage, current and resistance behave in it is what makes the more complicated circuits of the next chapter tractable.

concepts.name: IR drop
concepts.statement: Solving Ohm's law for the voltage gives $V = IR$, the voltage drop across a resistor produced by the current flowing through it, often called the $IR$ drop. Measure the voltage at various points in a circuit and you find that it increases at the voltage source and decreases at the resistor. In a simple circuit the same charge flows through each, so conservation of energy requires the voltage supplied by the source to equal the voltage dropped across the resistor.

concepts.name: Resistivity
concepts.statement: For a given shape, the resistance depends on the material the object is made of, and the resistivity is the property that carries that dependence. Resistivity is an intrinsic property of a material, independent of its shape or size, and its unit is the ohm-meter.

concepts.name: Resistance of a cylinder
concepts.statement: The resistance of a uniform cylinder is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its cross-sectional area, just as the resistance a pipe offers to fluid flow is: the longer the cylinder, the more collisions the charges make with its atoms, and the greater its diameter, the more current it can carry. With the resistivity of the material this gives the resistance of any simple shape from its dimensions alone.

concepts.name: Conductors, semiconductors and insulators
concepts.statement: The materials of Table 20.1 fall into three groups by their resistivities. Conductors have the smallest resistivities and varying but large free charge densities. Insulators have the largest, because most of their charges are bound to atoms and are not free to move. Semiconductors are intermediate: they have far fewer free charges than conductors, but the number depends strongly on the type and amount of impurities present, and modern electronics rests on that property.

concepts.name: Superconductivity
concepts.statement: The resistivity of all materials depends on temperature, and some become superconductors, with zero resistivity, at very low temperatures. A sample of mercury has no resistance at all up to about 4.2 K, and above that critical temperature its resistance makes a sudden jump and then increases nearly linearly. A material with no resistance carries a steady current with no continual supply of energy, which is why the possibility matters far beyond the laboratory.

concepts.name: Temperature coefficient of resistivity
concepts.statement: The temperature coefficient of resistivity is the empirical quantity that describes how much a material's resistivity changes with temperature. It is positive for metals, because at higher temperatures their atoms vibrate more rapidly and over larger distances, so the electrons make more collisions. It is negative for the semiconductors of Table 20.2, because increased thermal agitation there frees more charges to carry current. Some alloys, such as manganin, have a coefficient close to zero, which makes them ideal for a temperature-independent resistance standard.

concepts.name: Resistivity and temperature
concepts.statement: Over relatively small temperature changes, about 100 °C or less, the resistivity varies linearly with the temperature change, where $\rho_0$ is the original resistivity and $\alpha$ is the temperature coefficient. For larger changes the coefficient may itself vary or a nonlinear equation may be needed, so treat the linear form as the approximation it is.

concepts.name: Resistance and temperature
concepts.statement: Since the resistance of a cylinder is proportional to the resistivity, and since the length and the area change far less with temperature than the resistivity does, the resistance of an object has the same temperature dependence as the resistivity. Numerous thermometers are based on this effect, the most common being the thermistor, a semiconductor crystal with a strong temperature dependence whose resistance is measured to obtain its temperature.

concepts.name: Electric power
concepts.statement: Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is supplied by a source or dissipated by a device. Since electric energy is $\text{PE} = qV$, the power is the charge per second times the voltage, which is the current times the voltage, $P = IV$. One ampere-volt is one watt.

concepts.name: Power and resistance
concepts.statement: Substituting Ohm's law into $P = IV$ gives two further expressions, and each yields its own insight. The first says that the lower the resistance connected to a given voltage source, the greater the power delivered. Because the voltage is squared, raising it has a larger effect than expected, which is why a 25-W bulb connected to 240 V glows brightly and burns out. The second is the form to use when the current rather than the voltage is fixed, as in a transmission line. The first expression is always valid; these two can be used only for resistors.

concepts.name: Power supplied and dissipated
concepts.statement: In a circuit with one voltage source and a single resistor, the power supplied by the source and the power dissipated by the resistor are identical, because the resistor is the only place the energy can go. In more complicated circuits $P$ may be the power dissipated by a single device rather than the total power in the circuit, so always say which power you mean.

concepts.name: Electrical energy and cost
concepts.statement: Since power is energy per unit time, the energy a device uses is its power multiplied by the time it is on, and that is what appears on an electric bill. The energy unit on electric bills is the kilowatt-hour, which is $3.6\times10^{6}$ J, and the cost of running anything can be estimated from its power rating in kilowatts, the hours it is on and the cost per kilowatt-hour.

concepts.name: Lighting efficiency
concepts.statement: You can reduce the electrical energy used either by shortening the time of use or by lowering the power consumption. Lighting is one of the fastest places to do it, since it takes about 20 per cent of a home's energy use and closer to 40 per cent of a commercial building's. Fluorescent lights are about four times more efficient than incandescent lights and last up to ten times longer. White LED lights are about twice as efficient again and last five times longer than compact fluorescents.

concepts.name: Direct current
concepts.statement: Direct current is the flow of electric charge in only one direction, and it is the steady state of a constant-voltage circuit such as one driven by a battery. Naming it is what makes the contrast with alternating current sharp, and most of the examples of the chapter so far have been of this kind.

concepts.name: Alternating current
concepts.statement: Alternating current is the flow of electric charge that periodically reverses direction, and when the source varies sinusoidally the circuit is an alternating current circuit. The voltage between the terminals is $V = V_0\sin 2\pi ft$, where $V_0$ is the peak voltage and $f$ the frequency in hertz. In a simple resistance circuit the current follows it in phase as $I = I_0\sin 2\pi ft$ with $I_0 = V_0/R$. Most of the commercial and residential power we use is of this kind.

concepts.name: Average AC power
concepts.statement: Since the power supplied is the product of the current and the voltage and the two are in phase, the power is $I_0V_0\sin^2 2\pi ft$, which is never negative and fluctuates between zero and $I_0V_0$ twice in each cycle. We are most often concerned with the average rather than the fluctuation, and the average is half the peak, as is evident from the graph, since the areas above and below the half-peak line are equal.

concepts.name: rms current and voltage
concepts.statement: The ordinary average of an alternating current is zero, so we need a different kind of average: square the quantity, find its mean, and take the square root. The result is the root mean square. It is standard practice to quote the rms current and voltage and the average power rather than the peak values, so household electricity described as 120 V AC has an rms voltage of 120 V and a peak of about 170 V. Think of these as the equivalent DC values for a simple resistive circuit.

concepts.name: Ohm’s law for AC
concepts.statement: For alternating current, Ohm's law and the expressions for power are completely analogous to those for direct current, provided you use rms and average values throughout. That is what makes the rms average worth defining: with it, everything from 20.2 and 20.4 carries over unchanged.

concepts.name: High-voltage transmission
concepts.statement: Economies of scale make a few very large generating plants cheaper than many small ones, so power must travel long distances, and the energy lost on the way must be kept small. For a given power, raising the voltage lowers the current, and since the loss in a fixed-resistance line is $I^2R$, the loss falls as the square. 100 MW sent at 200 kV over a 1.00-Ω line loses a quarter of a per cent, while the same power at 25 kV loses 16 per cent. Alternating voltages are much easier to raise and lower than direct ones, which is why AC has prevailed in large-scale distribution.

concepts.name: AC voltage
concepts.statement: An AC voltage is a voltage that fluctuates sinusoidally with time, $V = V_0\sin 2\pi ft$, where $V_0$ is its peak value and $f$ its frequency.

concepts.name: rms current
concepts.statement: The rms current is the root mean square of an alternating current, $I_\text{rms} = I_0/\sqrt{2}$, where $I_0$ is the peak current.

concepts.name: rms voltage
concepts.statement: The rms voltage is the root mean square of an AC voltage, $V_\text{rms} = V_0/\sqrt{2}$, where $V_0$ is the peak voltage.

concepts.name: Thermal hazards
concepts.statement: A thermal hazard is one in which excessive electric power causes undesired thermal effects, such as starting a fire in the wall of a house. Electric power causes such heating whenever electric energy turns into thermal energy faster than it can safely be dissipated. Keeping this hazard separate from shock makes clear that different quantities govern the two.

concepts.name: Short circuit
concepts.statement: A short circuit is a low-resistance path between the terminals of a voltage source, such as the one made when worn insulation lets two wires touch. Because the resistance of the short is very small and the power dissipated in it is $V^2/r$, that power is very large: 120 V across 0.100 Ω gives 144 kW, far more than any household appliance uses, and thermal energy delivered at that rate very quickly melts or ignites the surrounding materials. Worse, the heating can ionize the material and lower the resistance further, raising the power again.

concepts.name: Overloaded wires
concepts.statement: A less dramatic thermal hazard occurs when the wires supplying a user carry too great a current, since the power dissipated in them is $I^2R_\text{w}$: a worn cord with 2.00 Ω rather than the 0.100 Ω it should have dissipates 200 W when 10.0 A passes through it. Fuses and circuit breakers limit such currents by opening the circuit automatically when a sustained current exceeds safe limits, a fuse by melting a metal strip and a breaker by bending a bimetallic strip that trips a spring.

concepts.name: Shock hazards
concepts.statement: A shock hazard occurs when electric current passes through a person, and the effects range from painful but otherwise harmless to heart-stopping. Current through people is not always harmful and is sometimes useful, since it can block back pain, burn off warts, drive a pacemaker or bring a heart out of fibrillation; what decides the outcome is the amount of the current, the path it takes, the duration of the shock and the frequency of the current.

concepts.name: Effects of current on the body
concepts.statement: Once the path, duration and frequency are fixed, current is the major factor determining the severity of a shock. The threshold of sensation is only 1 mA, and shocks below 5 mA are apparently harmless. From 10 to 20 mA the current stimulates sustained muscular contraction, so the hand closes on the wire and cannot let go. Between 100 and 300 mA ventricular fibrillation is possible and often fatal, and above about 300 mA burns begin. At several amperes the heart and diaphragm contract for the duration of the shock and often return to normal afterwards, which is how a defibrillator works. The body is most sensitive near the 50 and 60 Hz in common use and becomes progressively less sensitive at higher frequencies.

concepts.name: Body resistance and microshock
concepts.statement: A larger voltage is more hazardous, but since $I = V/R$ the severity of a shock depends on the combination of voltage and resistance, so no voltage is hazardous without knowing the resistance. Most of the body's resistance is in its dry skin, about 200 kΩ hand to foot, and 120 V drives only 0.6 mA through it. The same person soaking wet may have 10.0 kΩ and take 12 mA, above the can't-let-go threshold. When an intravenous infusion, a catheter or exposed pacemaker leads bypass the skin, the person is microshock sensitive, and currents about a thousandth of those in Table 20.3 produce similar effects.

concepts.name: Microshock sensitivity
concepts.statement: A person is microshock sensitive when the resistance of the skin is bypassed, possibly by a medical procedure, so that a very small current can reach the heart.

concepts.name: Resting potential
concepts.statement: A cell membrane separates electrically neutral fluids whose concentrations of sodium, potassium and chlorine ions differ, and it is semipermeable, passing potassium and chlorine in the resting state but not sodium. Diffusion carries those ions across until the layers of charge they build up stop further transfer by the Coulomb force, leaving two layers of charge right on the membrane and a potential difference of 70 to 90 mV across it. Because the membrane is only about 8 nm thick, that small voltage makes a field on the order of 11 MV/m, which has fundamental effects on the membrane's structure and permeability.

concepts.name: Action potential
concepts.statement: Any stimulus that changes the membrane's permeability creates a current along it. The membrane becomes temporarily permeable to sodium, which rushes in driven both by diffusion and by the Coulomb force and first neutralizes and then reverses the inside of the membrane, which is depolarization; the depolarization closes the membrane to sodium again and the movement of potassium returns the cell to its resting potential, which is repolarization. The sequence is a voltage pulse called the action potential, and only small fractions of the ions move, so the cell can fire hundreds of times before the sodium-potassium pump must restore the concentrations by active transport.

concepts.name: How a nerve impulse propagates
concepts.statement: An action potential is a voltage pulse at one place on a membrane, and the changing voltage and electric fields there alter the permeability of the adjacent membrane, so the same process happens next door, and then farther down. The result is a nerve impulse that moves along the cell membrane at about 1 m/s, slowly in electrical terms, and although it is due to sodium and potassium crossing the membrane it is equivalent to a wave of charge moving along the outside and inside of it.

concepts.name: Myelin sheath
concepts.statement: Myelin, a fatty insulator broken by unmyelinated gaps called nodes of Ranvier, sheathes some axons. Because myelin is an insulator, it keeps signals from jumping between adjacent nerves. The myelinated regions carry the signal at high speed as an ordinary conductor would, with no action potential and so no cell energy used. There is an $IR$ signal loss in the myelin, but each gap restores the signal to full voltage. A myelinated axon therefore transmits an impulse faster, with less energy and with better protection from cross talk. Destruction of the sheaths impairs transmission, as it does in multiple sclerosis.

concepts.name: Electrocardiogram
concepts.statement: The depolarization that makes a muscle cell contract can stimulate the cells next to it, so a depolarization wave crosses the heart from the sinoatrial node and coordinates its rhythmic contractions. An electrocardiogram is a record of the voltages that wave and the repolarization after it create, read as vector components between pairs of electrodes on the body. In the lead II potential the P wave is the depolarization of the atria, the QRS complex the depolarization of the ventricles, and the T wave their repolarization, with the systolic blood pressure following shortly after the QRS complex.

concepts.name: Bioelectricity
concepts.statement: Bioelectricity is the electrical effects in and created by biological systems. Nerve cells carry electrical signals, and the currents that make muscles contract produce voltages that can be measured outside the body.

concepts.name: Series connection
concepts.statement: Resistors are in series whenever the flow of charge must pass through them one after the other, so that there is only one path and every resistor carries the same current. The book's own example is a person holding a screwdriver: the shaft, the handle, the body and the shoes are four resistances the same current must cross in turn. Recognizing the connection is what decides which of the two combination rules applies, so it comes before either of them.

concepts.name: Resistance in series
concepts.statement: Since all of the current must pass through each resistor, it meets the resistance of each in turn, and the resistances simply add. The result follows from conservation of energy: the energy the source gives a charge is the energy the resistors take from it, so the source's voltage is the sum of the voltage drops, and dividing by the common current leaves the sum of the resistances. It is the rule that says a longer cord or a thicker sole reduces the current.

concepts.name: Voltage division in series
concepts.statement: The energy supplied to a charge by the source is the energy the resistors take from it, since there is nowhere else for the energy to go. Writing that energy as $qV$ on both sides and canceling the charge leaves the voltage of the source as the sum of the voltage drops across the resistors. Individual resistors in series do not each get the source's whole voltage; they divide it in proportion to their resistances.

concepts.name: Parallel connection
concepts.statement: Resistors are in parallel when each one is connected directly to the voltage source by wires of negligible resistance, so that each has the full voltage of the source across it and draws the current it would draw if it were alone. That is why a house, a car and every power distribution system is wired in parallel: each device gets the same voltage and works independently of the others.

concepts.name: Resistance in parallel
concepts.statement: Each branch has the source's full voltage, so the current in each is that voltage divided by its own resistance, and conservation of charge makes the source's current the sum of the branch currents. Factoring the voltage out of the sum leaves the reciprocals of the resistances adding, which is the rule for a parallel connection. Adding a branch adds a path, so it always raises the current and lowers the total resistance.

concepts.name: Current division in parallel
concepts.statement: Charge is conserved, so whatever current the source drives out must be exactly the current the branches carry between them. Parallel resistors do not each get the total current; they divide it, and the smallest resistance takes the largest share. This is the statement conservation of charge makes about a parallel connection, as the sum of the voltages is the statement conservation of energy makes about a series one.

concepts.name: Least resistance of a parallel combination
concepts.statement: When resistors are connected in parallel, more current flows from the source than would flow through any one of them alone, so the total resistance must be lower than the lowest of them. The reciprocals add, and a sum of reciprocals is larger than any one of them, so its inverse is smaller than the smallest resistance. It is the result that decides whether a circuit has been reduced correctly, since a parallel total larger than one of its parts is an arithmetic mistake.

concepts.name: Reducing a resistor network
concepts.statement: More complex connections of resistors are often just combinations of series and parallel parts, and wire resistance in series with parallel devices makes this case a common one. Identify the parts, replace each with its equivalent, and repeat until a single resistance remains. The process is more time consuming than difficult, and it lets you apply Ohm's law to a circuit that is not one loop.

concepts.name: IR drop in wires
concepts.statement: Wire resistance sits in series with the devices it feeds, so the current the devices draw produces an $IR$ drop in the wires and the voltage left for the devices is less than the source's. When a device of very low resistance switches on, the large current it draws makes that drop large, and everything else on the same wires receives less voltage. It is why the refrigerator light dims when the motor comes on and why a worn or very long extension cord wastes power.

concepts.name: Resistor
concepts.statement: A resistor is a component made to have a definite resistance, and in a circuit diagram every device that converts electrical energy, from a lamp to a heater, is drawn as one.

concepts.name: Electromotive force
concepts.statement: Every voltage source, whether it is a battery, a generator, a solar cell or a thermoelectric device, creates a potential difference that can drive current through a resistance. That potential difference, measured when no current flows, is called the electromotive force, or emf. Emf is not a force at all; it is a special type of potential difference, and its unit is the volt. It is set by the source's construction, such as the particular combination of chemicals in a battery.

concepts.name: Internal resistance
concepts.statement: Every voltage source has two fundamental parts, a source of electrical energy and an internal resistance, and the two are in series. The internal resistance is the inherent resistance to the flow of current within the source itself, and the smaller it is for a given emf, the more current and the more power the source can supply. It is why a truck battery and a motorcycle battery of the same emf are not interchangeable, and it rises as a battery is depleted.

concepts.name: Terminal voltage
concepts.statement: The voltage measured across a source's terminals is its emf less the voltage drop across its own internal resistance, so the larger the current drawn, or the larger the internal resistance, the smaller the terminal voltage. Terminal voltage equals emf only when no current flows. This one equation explains why car lights dim gradually as a battery runs down instead of blinking off, and why a battery tester measures the voltage under a load.

concepts.name: Current delivered to a load
concepts.statement: The internal resistance is in series with the load, so the total resistance of the circuit is the load plus the internal resistance and Ohm's law gives the current. The smaller the internal resistance, the greater the current a source supplies to a given load. When a battery ages and its internal resistance becomes a significant fraction of the load, the current falls noticeably, which is what a worn battery in a flashlight or a starter motor shows.

concepts.name: Sources in series
