concepts.statement: The hertz is the SI unit of frequency, one cycle per second, named for Heinrich Hertz, who first generated and detected electromagnetic waves.

concepts.name: Radiation from accelerated charges
concepts.statement: Whenever a current varies, the electric and magnetic fields around it vary, and the variation moves out from the source as a wave. The general statement is simpler still: accelerating charges radiate. That is why an alternating source drives a broadcast antenna, why an unshielded circuit leaks energy, and why a microwave oven has an antenna carrying an oscillating current.

concepts.name: Antenna electric field over one cycle
concepts.statement: An alternating source at the centre of a straight wire drives charge to one end and then to the other. At the instant of greatest separation, the electric field beside the antenna is greatest. A quarter of a cycle later the charges have met in the middle and the field there is zero, while the earlier maximum has already travelled away at $\kc$. One full cycle shows where the wave's shape comes from. How far the charges separate sets its amplitude, and how long the source takes to complete a cycle sets its wavelength, so a high frequency makes a short wave.

concepts.name: Magnetic part of the wave
concepts.statement: The same charges that separate along the antenna are a current while they move, and by Ampere's law a current makes a magnetic field, whose lines circle the wire. As the current varies, that field varies with it and propagates away at the speed of light, exactly as the electric field does. The magnetic part has the same period and the same wavelength as the electric part, because the same motion of the same charges makes both.

concepts.name: Transverse electromagnetic wave
concepts.statement: The two fields of the wave lie in different planes. The electric field oscillates in one plane, the magnetic field in a plane at right angles to it, and the wave travels along the line where the two planes meet. Both fields are therefore perpendicular to the direction of propagation, which makes an electromagnetic wave transverse. The two are also exactly in phase: they reach their maxima together and pass through zero together. This arrangement decides how a wave couples to a receiving wire or loop, so learn to picture it from any angle.

concepts.name: Ratio of field strengths
concepts.statement: The stronger the electric field made by the separated charge, the greater the current that flows and so the greater the magnetic field, so the two field strengths ought to rise and fall together. They do, and the constant ratio between them is the speed of light itself, at every instant and at every point in space. Because $\kc$ is such a large number, the result also says that the magnetic part of any electromagnetic wave is very weak beside the electric part.

concepts.name: Finding one field strength from the other
concepts.statement: Rearranging the ratio gives either field from the other in one step, and this is the calculation the section's problems ask for over and over. Dividing a field of 1000 V/m by the speed of light leaves a few microtesla, less than a tenth of the Earth's own weak field, which is the concrete form of the statement that the magnetic part of a wave is small. Checking that the units of volts per metre divided by metres per second really are teslas is worth doing once.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic wave in a medium
concepts.statement: Outside a vacuum an electromagnetic wave is slower, by the factor the medium's index of refraction names. The ratio of the field strengths is reduced in exactly the same proportion, so in a medium it is the wave's own speed, not the speed of light, that the two fields stand in. The result matters wherever a wave is not travelling through empty space, which is most of the places a reader will meet one.

concepts.name: Antenna resonance
concepts.statement: An antenna is not a circuit with a complete path. It is a wire on which the driving source sets up a standing wave of charge, and its dimensions decide the frequency at which it radiates best. That is a resonance, and tuning a radio or a television means changing electrical properties until the resonant condition is met. A receiving antenna works the same way in reverse. An arriving wave accelerates the electrons in it and sets up a standing wave that the set amplifies, so it too must resonate at the frequencies it should catch.

concepts.name: Oscillation
concepts.statement: To oscillate is to fluctuate back and forth in a steady beat, as the charges in an antenna do and as the fields of the wave they send out do.

concepts.name: Wave equation for light
concepts.statement: Propagation speed, frequency and wavelength are related for any wave by $\kvw = \kf\klam$, and for an electromagnetic wave in a vacuum the propagation speed is always the speed of light. Since $\kc$ never changes, the frequency and the wavelength can only trade against each other: the greater the frequency, the smaller the wavelength. This one relation is what lets the whole spectrum be laid out on a single axis and read in either unit.

concepts.name: Finding a wavelength or frequency
concepts.statement: Rearranged, the relation gives $\klam = \kc/\kf$, and this is the arithmetic that most of the section's problems come down to. An AM carrier of 1530 kHz is nearly 200 m long, an FM carrier of 105.1 MHz is 2.85 m, and a cell phone's 1.90 GHz signal is 15.8 cm; those three numbers explain why an AM mast is enormous and a phone's antenna is hidden inside the case. Carrying the units through as cycles per second keeps the answer in metres.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic spectrum
concepts.statement: All electromagnetic waves are the same phenomenon, and only frequency, and therefore wavelength, separates a radio wave from a gamma ray. Sorting them by frequency gives the named bands, radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray and gamma ray, over a remarkable range of frequencies and wavelengths. Some of the dividing lines are sharp and others are not. Where two bands overlap, the name of a wave depends on how it was made rather than on how fast it oscillates.

concepts.name: Rules of thumb for the spectrum
concepts.statement: Three statements hold across the whole spectrum and are worth carrying: a higher-frequency wave is more energetic and penetrates better, a higher-frequency wave carries more information in a given time, and the shorter the wavelength of a wave used to probe something, the smaller the detail it can resolve. Each has exceptions — magnetic resonance imaging uses 3 m radio waves to see detail smaller than a millimetre — and knowing that the rules are rules of thumb is part of knowing them.

concepts.name: Transmission, reflection and absorption
concepts.statement: When a wave meets a material, it may pass through, turn back, or be absorbed, and usually some of each happens. How a material behaves depends on the material and the frequency together, not on the material alone. Glass passes visible light and stops ultraviolet, and skin stops visible light and passes X-rays. A substance is transparent or opaque only for a named band.

concepts.name: Radio waves and modulation
concepts.statement: Radio waves are defined by their source: any electromagnetic wave produced by currents in wires and circuits is one. To carry information, a station varies a carrier at its own frequency, either in amplitude, which is AM, or in frequency, which is FM. The receiver resonates at the carrier frequency and responds to whichever kind of variation it uses. Noise adds to amplitude, so an FM receiver can throw away what an AM receiver must treat as part of the signal, which makes FM the quieter of the two.

concepts.name: Most efficient antenna length
concepts.statement: An antenna radiates best when a standing wave fits on it, and for a linear antenna that length is $\klam/2$. With one end on the ground, a quarter wavelength does the same work, just as a tube closed at one end resonates at a quarter of its fundamental wavelength. The rule explains the sizes of antennas you see. An AM broadcast antenna must be hundreds of metres long, while an FM or mobile phone antenna is small enough to hide and goes high up for a clear line of sight.

concepts.name: Uses of microwaves
concepts.statement: Microwaves are the highest frequencies that currents in ordinary circuits can produce, from about $10^{9}$ Hz up to the highest practical $LC$ resonance near $10^{12}$ Hz, and their short wavelengths make them good for carrying information and for seeing detail. Radar finds a distance by timing an echo and a speed by the Doppler shift in it, and maps a planet through cloud that stops visible light. In a microwave oven the frequency is chosen so that polar molecules turning to follow the alternating field absorb the energy, which heats the food and not the plate, and the hot spots are an interference pattern.

concepts.name: Sources across the spectrum
concepts.statement: Each band comes from a process of a particular size. Accelerating charges in circuits give radio waves and microwaves. The thermal agitation of atoms and molecules, and their vibrations and rotations, give microwaves, infrared and some visible light. Electronic transitions within atoms and molecules give visible light and ultraviolet. Transitions of inner electrons and the braking of fast electrons in matter give X-rays, and the nucleus itself gives gamma rays. The source decides the name where two bands overlap, since an X-ray and a gamma ray of the same frequency differ only in origin.

concepts.name: Radiation and living tissue
concepts.statement: The higher the frequency, the more energy a wave delivers to whatever absorbs it, and above visible light that energy begins to break molecules apart. Ultraviolet-B excites and distorts DNA and causes skin cancer and cataracts, and the ozone layer is what keeps most of it off the surface; X-rays penetrate further and damage more, which is both their hazard and, aimed carefully, their use against cancer; gamma rays do the same at higher energies. The same properties make them useful: sterilization, vitamin D, imaging by shadow and by emission, and therapy.

concepts.name: Thermal agitation
concepts.statement: Thermal agitation is the thermal motion of the atoms and molecules of any object above absolute zero, which makes them emit and absorb radiation, mostly in the infrared.

concepts.name: Infrared radiation
concepts.statement: Infrared radiation is the band of the electromagnetic spectrum with frequencies from just below those of red light down to the microwaves.

concepts.name: Visible light
concepts.statement: Visible light is the narrow band of the electromagnetic spectrum to which the normal human eye responds, with wavelengths from about 380 nm to 760 nm.

concepts.name: Ultraviolet radiation
concepts.statement: Ultraviolet radiation is the band of the electromagnetic spectrum extending upward in frequency from violet light and overlapping the lowest x rays.

concepts.name: X rays
concepts.statement: X rays are invisible, penetrating electromagnetic radiation of very high frequency, overlapping the ultraviolet below and the gamma rays above.

concepts.name: Gamma rays
concepts.statement: Gamma rays are electromagnetic radiation of extremely high frequency, emitted by the nucleus of an atom in nuclear decay or in other nuclear and particle processes.

concepts.name: Carrier wave
concepts.statement: A carrier wave is an electromagnetic wave that carries a signal by the modulation of its amplitude or of its frequency.

concepts.name: Amplitude modulation
concepts.statement: Amplitude modulation places information on an electromagnetic wave by varying the amplitude of a carrier wave with the signal, while its frequency stays fixed.

concepts.name: Frequency modulation
concepts.statement: Frequency modulation places information on an electromagnetic wave by varying the frequency of a carrier wave with the signal, while its amplitude stays fixed.

concepts.name: Radar
concepts.statement: Radar is a common application of microwaves: it finds the distance to objects as diverse as clouds and aircraft from the time a reflected pulse takes to return.

concepts.name: Extremely low frequency
concepts.statement: Extremely low frequency radiation is electromagnetic radiation of the lowest frequencies, usually from 0 to 300 Hz but also up to about 1 kHz.

concepts.name: Television
concepts.statement: Television carries video and audio signals on electromagnetic waves, broadcast in the radio band.

concepts.name: Very high frequency
concepts.statement: Very high frequency TV channels use frequencies in the two ranges from 54 to 88 MHz and from 174 to 222 MHz.

concepts.name: Ultra-high frequency
concepts.statement: Ultra-high frequency TV channels use frequencies above those of VHF, from 470 to 1000 MHz.

concepts.name: Wave energy and field amplitude
concepts.statement: A wave brings energy into a system because its fields exert forces on charges and move them, and the larger the fields, the more work they can do. For waves of every kind the energy goes as the amplitude squared, and for an electromagnetic wave the amplitude is the maximum field strength, so the energy goes as $\kEfo^2$ and as $\kBmago^2$. Doubling the fields quadruples the energy, which is the whole content of the section's first figure and the reason a microwave oven with half the field takes four times as long.

concepts.name: Average intensity from the electric amplitude
concepts.statement: Intensity is power per unit area, and for a continuous sinusoidal electromagnetic wave you can write it from the electric amplitude alone. The factor of a half comes from averaging the square of a sine over a cycle, and the speed of light and the permittivity of free space turn a field strength into a power per square metre. Use this form when the electric field is the quantity given or wanted.

concepts.name: Average intensity from the magnetic amplitude
concepts.statement: Substituting $\kBmag = \kEf/\kc$ and $\varepsilon_0 = 1/\mu_0\kc^2$ into the first expression gives the intensity in terms of the magnetic amplitude, and substituting only part of the way gives it in terms of both amplitudes at once. The three forms are not three results but one, written in whichever quantities a problem happens to supply, and the principle behind all three is the same: energy in a wave is related to amplitude squared.

concepts.name: Peak intensity
concepts.statement: The three expressions are written for a sinusoidal wave, and averaging the square of a sine over a cycle leaves half of its maximum. So the intensity at the crest of the wave is twice the average intensity the same expressions give, and a problem that asks for a peak rather than an average needs the factor of two. The same factor is why the root mean square field is the amplitude divided by the square root of two.

concepts.name: Finding field amplitudes from intensity
concepts.statement: The common problem of the section runs in one direction: a source of known power spreads it over a known area, which gives the intensity, and the intensity gives the electric amplitude by rearranging the first expression, after which dividing by the speed of light gives the magnetic amplitude. Doing it in that order avoids the awkward constants twice over, and the answers are worth a glance for size, since a kilowatt in an oven gives a field of a few kilovolts per metre and a few microtesla.

concepts.name: Maximum field strength
concepts.statement: The maximum field strength of an electromagnetic wave is the amplitude of its electric or magnetic field, the largest value the field reaches as it oscillates.

concepts.name: Eye as a single thin lens
concepts.statement: The cornea and lens of the eye can be treated as a single thin converging lens a fixed distance from the retina, on which it forms a real, inverted image. The thin lens equations then describe the eye, and every defect and correction becomes a question about that one lens.

concepts.name: Power of the cornea
concepts.statement: The largest change in refractive index, and so the greatest bending of light, is where light passes from air into the cornea, so the cornea supplies about two-thirds of the power of the eye and the lens the rest. This is why reshaping the cornea corrects vision.

concepts.name: Accommodation
concepts.statement: Accommodation is the ability of the eye to adjust its focal length. Because the lens-to-retina distance is fixed, the eye focuses on objects at different distances by changing the power of its lens.

concepts.name: Thin lens equations for the eye
concepts.statement: Written in terms of power, the thin lens equation for the eye is $P = 1/d_{\text{o}} + 1/d_{\text{i}}$, with the image distance fixed at the lens-to-retina distance, and the magnification is $h_{\text{i}}/h_{\text{o}} = -d_{\text{i}}/d_{\text{o}}$.

concepts.name: Finding an image on the retina
concepts.statement: To find the power the eye needs or the size of an image on the retina, set the image distance to the lens-to-retina distance, put every distance in meters, and apply the thin lens equations for the eye.

concepts.name: Presbyopia
concepts.statement: Presbyopia is a condition in which the lens of the eye becomes progressively unable to focus on objects close to the viewer, as the ability to accommodate shrinks with age. It is a loss of added power for close vision, and a converging lens supplies the missing power.

concepts.name: Nearsightedness and farsightedness
concepts.statement: Nearsightedness, or myopia, is a visual defect in which distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina; the eye has too much power. Farsightedness, or hyperopia, is the condition in which incoming rays reach the retina before they converge into a focused image; the eye has too little power for close objects.

concepts.name: Near point and far point
concepts.statement: The far point is the object point imaged on the retina by an unaccommodated eye, normally at infinity. The near point is the point nearest the eye at which an object is accurately focused on the retina at full accommodation, normally 25 cm away.

concepts.name: Correcting nearsightedness
concepts.statement: A diverging lens corrects nearsightedness by making an image of a distant object at the person's far point. Its power follows from the thin lens equation, with the image distance negative and measured from the spectacle.

concepts.name: Correcting farsightedness
concepts.statement: A converging lens corrects farsightedness by making an image of a close object at the person's near point, farther away than the object itself. Measure both distances from the spectacle and give the image distance its negative sign.

concepts.name: Astigmatism
concepts.statement: Astigmatism is the result of an inability of the cornea to focus an image properly onto the retina, a difference in the power of the eye along different axes. It is corrected with a cylindrical lens rather than a spherical one.

concepts.name: Power of lenses in contact
concepts.statement: The power of thin lenses placed close together is approximately the sum of their powers. This lets a contact lens, a tear layer or a reshaped cornea be treated as an addition to the power of the eye.

concepts.name: Laser vision correction
concepts.statement: Laser vision correction is a medical procedure that corrects myopia, hyperopia and astigmatism by reshaping the cornea, which supplies most of the power of the eye. The laser uses ultraviolet light, which the cornea absorbs strongly.

concepts.name: Myopia
concepts.statement: Myopia, or nearsightedness, is a visual defect in which distant objects appear blurred because their images are focused in front of the retina rather than on it.

concepts.name: Hyperopia
concepts.statement: Hyperopia, or farsightedness, is the condition of an eye in which incoming rays of light reach the retina before they converge into a focused image, so that close objects appear blurred.

concepts.name: Near point
concepts.statement: The near point is the point nearest the eye at which an object is accurately focused on the retina at full accommodation, normally 25 cm away.

concepts.name: Far point
concepts.statement: The far point is the object point imaged on the retina by an unaccommodated eye, normally at infinity.

concepts.name: Rods and cones
concepts.statement: Rods and cones are the two types of photoreceptors in the human retina. Rods are sensitive and colorless and serve vision at low light levels; cones are active at higher light levels, give color and fine detail, and crowd the fovea.

concepts.name: Simplified theory of color vision
concepts.statement: The simplified theory of color vision states that there are three primary colors, which correspond to the three types of cones, each sensitive to a different range of wavelengths. It explains how three colors of light can produce thousands of hues, though some evidence shows that it is incomplete.

concepts.name: True color of an object
concepts.statement: The true color of an object is set by the wavelengths it absorbs and reflects, a property of the object rather than of the light falling on it. From it we can predict how a colored object appears under light that is not white.

concepts.name: Color of a light source
concepts.statement: The color of a light source is set by the spectrum of wavelengths it emits, from the sharp line of a laser to the broad spectrum of the Sun.

concepts.name: Color constancy
concepts.statement: Color constancy is the part of the visual perception system that lets people perceive color consistently in a variety of conditions, so that a white tablecloth looks white under sunlight and under candlelight. The eye and brain achieve it by comparing an object with its surroundings.

concepts.name: Hue
concepts.statement: The hue of a color is its identity as it relates specifically to the spectrum, such as red, orange or blue.

concepts.name: Retinex theory
concepts.statement: The retinex theory explains color and brightness perception and their constancies as the work of both the retina and the cortex, whose names combine in its own. It accounts for the ability to perceive color in an ambient-colored environment.

concepts.name: Compound microscope
concepts.statement: A compound microscope is constructed from two convex lenses, the objective and the eyepiece. The objective forms a large real image, and that image is the object for the eyepiece, which magnifies it further as a magnifier does.

concepts.name: Overall magnification
concepts.statement: The overall magnification of a system of thin lenses and mirrors is the product of the magnifications of its elements, $m = m_{\text{o}}m_{\text{e}}$, since each element multiplies the height of the image it is given.

concepts.name: Solving a two-lens system
concepts.statement: To find the image and magnification of a system of two or more lenses, locate the image formed by the first lens, use its distance from the second lens as that lens's object distance, and so find the final image and the overall magnification.

concepts.name: Numerical aperture
concepts.statement: The numerical aperture of a lens, $\text{NA} = n \sin\alpha$, expresses its ability to gather light and to resolve fine detail, where $n$ is the index of refraction of the medium between the lens and the specimen and $\alpha$ is half the angle of acceptance.

concepts.name: f-number
concepts.statement: The $f$-number of a camera lens is its focal length divided by the diameter of its aperture, $f/\# = f/D \approx 1/(2\,\text{NA})$. A smaller $f$-number means a wider aperture and more light.

concepts.name: Immersion objectives
concepts.statement: Filling the gap between the specimen and the objective with oil or water lets rays that would have been refracted away enter the lens, which makes the numerical aperture larger than one.

concepts.name: Microscopes beyond visible light
concepts.statement: A specimen must be illuminated by transmission, scattering or reflection, and microscopes that use x rays or electrons in place of light resolve far finer detail with the same focusing physics.

concepts.name: Objective lens
concepts.statement: The objective lens of an optical instrument is the lens nearest to the object being examined.

concepts.name: Eyepiece
concepts.statement: The eyepiece of an optical instrument is the lens or combination of lenses nearest to the eye of the observer.

concepts.name: Image of a distant object
concepts.statement: For an object at a very great distance, the thin lens equation puts the image one focal length behind the objective, which fixes where the eyepiece of a telescope goes.

concepts.name: Angular magnification of a telescope
concepts.statement: The angular magnification of a telescope with two convex lenses is $M = \theta'/\theta = -f_{\text{o}}/f_{\text{e}}$, so a large magnification needs an objective of long focal length and an eyepiece of short focal length.

concepts.name: Upright and inverted telescopes
concepts.statement: A telescope of two convex lenses forms an inverted image. Galileo's concave eyepiece, or a third convex lens that inverts the image again, gives an upright one.

concepts.name: Reflecting telescopes
concepts.statement: A concave mirror can serve as the objective of a telescope. Mirrors can be made far larger than lenses, gather more light, reach long focal lengths and do not suffer from chromatic aberration.

concepts.name: Telescopes across the spectrum
concepts.statement: Telescopes are not limited to visible light: radio dishes and grazing-incidence x-ray mirrors extend them across the electromagnetic spectrum.

concepts.name: Angular magnification
concepts.statement: The angular magnification of an instrument is the ratio of the angle the image subtends at the eye to the angle the object subtends when viewed by the unaided eye.

concepts.name: Adaptive optics
concepts.statement: Adaptive optics is an optical technology in which computers adjust the lenses and mirrors of a device to correct rapidly changing distortions of the image, such as those the atmosphere causes in a telescope.

concepts.name: Chromatic aberration
concepts.statement: Chromatic aberration is the dependence of the focal length of a lens on the color of the light. Because the index of refraction depends on wavelength, a single lens brings violet light to a focus closer than red. Mirrors are free of it, and a doublet of two glasses partly corrects it.

concepts.name: Coma and spherical aberration
concepts.statement: Coma is the failure of rays from an off-axis object to meet at one point. Spherical aberration is the focusing of rays through the edge of a lens closer than rays near its axis. Both occur even in light of one color.

concepts.name: Reducing aberrations
concepts.statement: Aberrations are reduced by stopping down the aperture, by shaped surfaces, by systems of several elements, by graded index lenses and by correcting the image with a computer, at a cost in brightness or complexity.

concepts.name: Aberration
concepts.statement: An aberration is a failure of rays to converge at one focus because of limitations or defects in a lens or mirror.

concepts.name: Wave optics
concepts.statement: Wave optics is the branch of optics that considers the behavior of light when it exhibits wave characteristics, particularly when it interacts with objects not much larger than its wavelength, such as a narrow slit. Only waves explain effects such as the colors of a soap bubble or an oil slick.

concepts.name: Interference as the hallmark of a wave
concepts.statement: A ray passing through slits would continue straight ahead, while a wave spreads out and forms a pattern of bright and dark regions by interference. Such a pattern is the most certain indication that something is a wave, whether water, sound, light or even matter.

concepts.name: Wavelength in a medium
concepts.statement: When light enters a medium its speed drops to $c/n$ but its frequency stays fixed, so its wavelength shrinks by the same factor: $\lambda_n = \lambda/n$.

concepts.name: Color in a medium
concepts.statement: Light in a medium behaves like a forced oscillation that keeps the frequency of its source. Its speed and wavelength change, but its color does not, because color goes with frequency. Red light does not turn blue when it enters water.

concepts.name: Huygens’s principle
concepts.statement: Huygens's principle states that every point on a wavefront is a source of wavelets that spread out in the forward direction at the same speed as the wave itself. The new wavefront is a line tangent to all of the wavelets. This one construction explains reflection, refraction and diffraction.

concepts.name: Reflection and refraction from Huygens’s principle
concepts.statement: The laws of reflection and refraction were stated for rays in the previous chapter. Huygens’s construction shows why they hold: wavelets from a mirror leave in turn and build a wavefront at an angle equal to the incident one, and wavelets in a slower medium travel less far, so the wavefront turns toward the perpendicular.

concepts.name: Diffraction
concepts.statement: Diffraction is the bending of a wave around the edges of an opening or an obstacle. Sound fills a room through an open door while light casts a sharp shadow of the doorway, because the amount of bending depends on the ratio of the wavelength to the opening.

concepts.name: Diffraction and opening size
concepts.statement: How much a wave bends depends on the size of the opening compared with its wavelength. A wide opening lets the wavefront through almost straight, and a narrow one spreads it widely. This is the reason light behaves like a ray in everyday life and like a wave in a narrow slit.

concepts.name: Coherent and incoherent light
concepts.statement: Coherent waves are in phase or have a definite phase relationship, and they produce a steady pattern of interference. Incoherent waves have random phase relationships and produce none, as with the two headlights of a car.

concepts.name: Young’s double slit experiment
concepts.statement: In 1801 Thomas Young sent light through two narrow slits and found a pattern of many bright and dark lines rather than two lines. The waves from the two slits overlap and interfere, and the experiment gave definitive proof of the wave character of light.

concepts.name: Path length difference
concepts.statement: For a distant screen the paths from two slits a distance $d$ apart are nearly parallel, and the difference in their lengths to a point at angle $\theta$ is $\Delta l = d\sin\theta$.

concepts.name: Double slit constructive interference
terms: constructive interference for a double slit
concepts.statement: Bright fringes of a double slit appear where the path length difference is an integral multiple of the wavelength, $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$. The smaller the slit separation, the larger the angle of each fringe.

concepts.name: Double slit destructive interference
terms: destructive interference for a double slit
concepts.statement: Dark fringes of a double slit appear where the path length difference is a half-integral multiple of the wavelength, $d\sin\theta = (m + \tfrac{1}{2})\lambda$, so that crest meets trough.

concepts.name: Order of interference
concepts.statement: The order of an interference fringe is the integer $m$ in the conditions for constructive and destructive interference, the number of whole wavelengths by which its two paths differ. The central fringe is of order zero.

concepts.name: Finding a wavelength from a double slit pattern
concepts.statement: Interference patterns measure wavelength: solving $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ for whichever quantity is unknown gives a wavelength from a measured angle, or a slit separation from a known wavelength.

concepts.name: Finding the highest order
concepts.statement: Because $\sin\theta$ can be no larger than one, setting $\sin\theta = 1$ in the interference condition gives the largest order that reaches the screen.

concepts.name: Fringe spacing
concepts.statement: For small angles the fringes of a double slit are evenly spaced on a screen a distance $x$ away, with spacing $\Delta y = x\lambda/d$, which grows with the distance to the screen and the wavelength and shrinks with the slit separation.

concepts.name: Coherent light
concepts.statement: Waves are coherent when they are in phase or have a definite phase relationship.

concepts.name: Incoherent light
concepts.statement: Waves are incoherent when they have random phase relationships.

concepts.name: Diffraction grating
concepts.statement: A diffraction grating is a large number of evenly spaced parallel slits. It forms bright regions at the same angles as a double slit, and gratings work by transmission and by reflection. Opals, butterfly wings and bird feathers owe their colors to natural gratings.

concepts.name: Grating constructive interference
terms: constructive interference for a diffraction grating
concepts.statement: Each ray from a grating travels $d\sin\theta$ farther than its neighbor, so all of them arrive in phase when $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$, the same condition as for a double slit. The slits of a grating are closer, giving fewer maxima at larger angles.

concepts.name: Sharpness of grating maxima
concepts.statement: The bright regions of a grating are narrower and brighter, and its dark regions darker, than those of a double slit. The more slits there are, the sharper the maxima, which is why a grating can separate wavelengths that lie close together.

concepts.name: Finding a grating’s spectrum
concepts.statement: White light through a grating is spread into a rainbow in every order except the central one, with violet nearest the center. Find the angle of each wavelength from $d\sin\theta = m\lambda$ and then its position on the screen from $y = x\tan\theta$.

concepts.name: Single slit diffraction pattern
concepts.statement: Light from different parts of one slit interferes with itself. The result is a pattern whose central maximum is wider and much brighter than the dimmer maxima on either side, unlike the evenly spaced lines of a grating. The narrower the slit, the more the pattern spreads.

concepts.name: Single slit destructive interference
terms: destructive interference for a single slit
concepts.statement: A single slit of width $D$ has a minimum where the rays from its top and bottom differ in path by a whole number of wavelengths, $D\sin\theta = m\lambda$, since each ray from one half of the slit then has a partner from the other half that cancels it. There is no minimum of order zero.

concepts.name: Solving a single slit problem
concepts.statement: Solving D sin θ = mλ gives the width of a slit from the angle of one of its minima, or the angle of any other minimum once the width is known. The same condition applies to sound through a door and ocean waves through a harbor opening.

concepts.name: Diffraction limit on resolution
concepts.statement: Light through a circular aperture spreads into a fuzzy spot surrounded by rings, and the images of two close point sources overlap. Every lens, mirror and pupil has a finite diameter, so this limit to resolution is an inescapable consequence of the wave nature of light.

concepts.name: Rayleigh criterion
concepts.statement: By the Rayleigh criterion, two images are just resolvable when the center of the diffraction pattern of one lies on the first minimum of the other. For a circular aperture of diameter $D$ this occurs at $\theta = 1.22\lambda/D$ in radians, so a larger aperture or a shorter wavelength resolves finer detail.

concepts.name: Finding a resolvable separation
concepts.statement: Once the smallest resolvable angle is known, the distance between two objects that can just be told apart is that angle times their distance away, $s = r\theta$.

concepts.name: Diffraction spreading of a beam
concepts.statement: Even a beam of rays made as parallel as possible spreads out at an angle of about $1.22\lambda/D$ because its diameter is limited. The spreading can be reduced only by making the beam wider, which is why a laser sent to the Moon is first expanded through a telescope.

concepts.name: Resolving power of a lens
concepts.statement: The resolving power of a lens is the smallest distance between two points that can still be seen as distinct. The Rayleigh angle with the small angle approximation gives it as $x = 1.22\lambda d/D$, and the smaller it is, the greater the resolution.

concepts.name: Resolution and numerical aperture
concepts.statement: A lens with a larger numerical aperture collects more light, gives a brighter image and resolves finer detail: its resolving power is $x = 0.61\lambda n/\text{NA}$. A larger numerical aperture also makes the focal spot smaller, which in wave optics is never a true point.

concepts.name: Thin film interference
concepts.statement: Thin film interference is the interference between light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of a thin film. The ray that enters the film travels farther and may return in or out of phase with the ray reflected at the top, so different thicknesses favor different colors, as in a soap bubble or an oil slick.

concepts.name: Phase change on reflection
concepts.statement: Light reflecting from a medium with a greater index of refraction than the one it travels in undergoes a 180° phase change, a shift of $\lambda/2$. Light reflecting from a medium of smaller index undergoes none.

concepts.name: Applying thin film conditions
concepts.statement: For light incident perpendicularly, the ray reflected from the bottom of a film travels about $2t$ farther, measured in wavelengths in the film. Combine that path difference with the phase changes at the two surfaces: a total shift of a whole number of wavelengths is constructive, and a half-integral number is destructive.

concepts.name: Designing a non-reflective coating
concepts.statement: A thin layer on a lens can make the light reflected from its two surfaces cancel. When both reflections carry a phase change, the thinnest such coating is a quarter of the wavelength in the film thick, $t = (\lambda/n_2)/4$.

concepts.name: Air wedges and Newton’s rings
concepts.statement: A film whose thickness changes steadily shows a band of color, or of light and dark in pure light, for every step of one wavelength. Two microscope slides with a hair between them, or a lens pressed on a flat blank, show these bands, which lets a lens be ground to an accuracy of less than a wavelength.

concepts.name: Polarization of light
concepts.statement: Polarization is the attribute that the oscillations of a wave have a definite direction relative to its direction of propagation. Light is a transverse wave, and polarized light has its electric and magnetic field oscillations in a definite direction. Only a transverse wave can be polarized.

concepts.name: Polarizing filters
concepts.statement: A polarizing filter passes only the component of the electric field parallel to its axis, so the light leaving it is polarized. Two filters with crossed axes pass nothing at all.

concepts.name: Malus’s law
concepts.statement: A polarizing filter passes only the component $E\cos\theta$ of a polarized wave's field, and since intensity goes as the square of the amplitude, the transmitted intensity is $I = I_0\cos^2\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the direction of polarization and the axis of the filter.

concepts.name: Polarization by reflection
concepts.statement: Light reflected from water or glass is partly polarized, more horizontally than vertically, because the vertically polarized part is preferentially refracted. Polaroid sunglasses with vertical axes therefore cut glare.

concepts.name: Brewster’s law
concepts.statement: Brewster's law states that the reflected light is completely polarized when the angle of reflection is Brewster's angle, $\tan\theta_{\text{b}} = n_2/n_1$, where $n_1$ is the index of the medium in which the incident and reflected light travel and $n_2$ the index of the medium that reflects it.

concepts.name: Polarization by scattering
concepts.statement: Sunlight shakes the electrons of air molecules perpendicular to its direction of travel, and they radiate like small antennae, so light scattered at right angles to the original ray is polarized. This is why the blue sky grows bright and dim through rotating polarizing sunglasses.

concepts.name: Liquid crystals, optical activity and birefringence
concepts.statement: Some materials act on the direction of polarization itself. A liquid crystal rotates it by 90° unless a voltage is applied, which is how a pixel of an LCD works; optically active substances such as sugar water rotate it; stressed plastic shows colored patterns between crossed filters; and a birefringent crystal splits a beam in two.

concepts.name: Axis of a polarizing filter
concepts.statement: The axis of a polarizing filter is the direction along which the filter passes the electric field of an electromagnetic wave.

concepts.name: Direction of polarization
concepts.statement: The direction of polarization of an electromagnetic wave is defined to be the direction parallel to its electric field.

concepts.name: Horizontal and vertical polarization
concepts.statement: Light is horizontally polarized when its oscillations are in a horizontal plane, and vertically polarized when they are in a vertical plane.

concepts.name: Unpolarized light
concepts.statement: Unpolarized light is made of waves that are randomly polarized, with every direction of polarization. The Sun and most other sources produce unpolarized light.

concepts.name: Brewster’s angle
concepts.statement: Brewster's angle is the angle of reflection at which the reflected light is completely polarized, $\theta_{\text{b}} = \tan^{-1}(n_2/n_1)$.

concepts.name: Optically active substance
concepts.statement: An optically active substance rotates the plane of polarization of light passing through it. Sugar water is an example, and the amount of rotation measures its concentration.

concepts.name: Birefringence
concepts.statement: A birefringent crystal splits an unpolarized beam of light into two beams, which are polarized in different directions.

concepts.name: Completely polarized reflected light
terms: reflected light that is completely polarized
concepts.statement: Reflected light is completely polarized when it is reflected at Brewster's angle $\theta_{\text{b}}$.

concepts.name: Wavelength limit of microscopy
concepts.statement: Because light diffracts around small objects, no microscope using light can show details much smaller than its wavelength. Shorter wavelengths, as in ultraviolet microscopes, show finer detail.

concepts.name: Interference and phase-contrast microscopy
concepts.statement: Light passing through an object of different index emerges out of phase with light from the background, and superimposing the two makes the difference visible as contrast. Interference microscopes and phase-contrast microscopes enhance the contrast of nearly transparent objects in this way.

concepts.name: Confocal microscope
concepts.statement: A confocal microscope uses the extended focal region of wave optics and a pinhole that blocks light from points out of focus. Scanning the pinhole sideways and then up and down builds a three-dimensional image of a thick specimen, even of live cells in motion.

concepts.name: Contrast
concepts.statement: Contrast is the difference in intensity between objects and the background on which they are observed.

concepts.name: Polarization microscope
concepts.statement: A polarization microscope enhances contrast by using the polarization of light, which makes it useful for objects that are optically active.

concepts.name: Ultraviolet microscope
concepts.statement: An ultraviolet microscope is built with special lenses that transmit ultraviolet rays, and it records its images by photographic or electronic means. Its shorter wavelength shows finer detail than visible light can.

concepts.name: Interference microscope
concepts.statement: An interference microscope enhances the contrast between objects and background by superimposing a reference beam of light upon the light emerging from the sample.

concepts.name: Phase-contrast microscope
concepts.statement: A phase-contrast microscope uses wave interference and differences in phase to enhance contrast.

concepts.name: Relativity
concepts.statement: Relativity is the study of how different observers measure the same event. Galileo and Newton gave the classical answer, and Einstein the modern one, divided into special relativity for observers moving at constant velocity and general relativity for observers who accelerate.

concepts.name: First postulate of special relativity
concepts.statement: The first postulate of special relativity states that the laws of physics are the same and can be stated in their simplest form in all inertial frames of reference. There is no preferred frame and no absolute motion.

concepts.name: Michelson-Morley experiment
concepts.statement: In 1887 Michelson and Morley looked for a change in the speed of light due to the Earth's motion through a supposed medium for light, and found none. The result showed that light needs no medium and that the speed of light in a vacuum is the same in all frames of reference.

concepts.name: Second postulate of special relativity
concepts.statement: The second postulate of special relativity states that the speed of light in a vacuum has the same value $\kc$ for every observer, whatever the motion of the source or the observer.

concepts.name: Special relativity
concepts.statement: Special relativity is the theory of how observers in inertial frames of reference, moving at constant velocity relative to one another, measure the same events. Einstein built it on two postulates.

concepts.name: Relativity of simultaneity
concepts.statement: Two events that are simultaneous for one observer need not be simultaneous for another who moves relative to the first. The elapsed time between two events can therefore depend on who measures it.

concepts.name: Time dilation
concepts.statement: Time dilation is the phenomenon of time passing more slowly for an observer who is moving relative to another observer. Light crossing a moving ship travels a longer, slanted path in the frame of an observer on the Earth, and since its speed is the same in both frames, that observer measures more time for the same process. All clocks moving relative to an observer, biological clocks included, are observed to run slow.

concepts.name: Proper time
concepts.statement: Proper time $\Delta t_0$ is the time measured by an observer at rest relative to the event being observed. It is the shortest elapsed time any observer measures for that event.

concepts.name: Relativistic factor
concepts.statement: The relativistic factor is $\gamma = 1/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}$. It is 1 at rest, stays very nearly 1 at everyday speeds and grows without limit as $v$ approaches $c$, and it sets the size of every relativistic effect.

concepts.name: Time dilation equation
concepts.statement: The time an observer moving relative to an event measures for it is the proper time multiplied by the relativistic factor, $\Delta t = \Delta t_0/\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = \gamma\Delta t_0$. At low velocities the two times are nearly equal.

concepts.name: Calculating time dilation
concepts.statement: To find a dilated time, decide which time is proper, find $\gamma$ from the speed, and multiply. Run the other way, the equation gives the relative speed from two measured times.

concepts.name: Twin paradox
concepts.statement: The twin paradox asks why a twin who travels at a relativistic speed away from the Earth and back ages less than the twin who stays at home, when from the traveler's frame the Earth seems to move. The premise is faulty: the traveler accelerates and the twin at home does not, and special relativity does not apply to accelerating frames.

concepts.name: Agreement on relative speed
concepts.statement: Two observers who disagree about elapsed time still agree about how fast they move relative to each other. Since speed is distance divided by time, a disagreement about time forces a disagreement about distance.

concepts.name: Proper length
concepts.statement: Proper length $L_0$ is the distance between two points measured by an observer who is at rest relative to both of them. Earth-bound observers measure proper length when they measure the distance between two points at rest on the Earth.

concepts.name: Length contraction equation
concepts.statement: Length contraction is the shortening of the measured length of an object moving relative to the observer's frame, $L = L_0\sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2} = L_0/\gamma$. It occurs only along the direction of motion.

concepts.name: Calculating length contraction
concepts.statement: To find a contracted length, name the proper length, find $\gamma$, and divide. Run the other way, the equation gives the speed that makes a given length appear shorter.

concepts.name: Relativity at everyday speeds
concepts.statement: At speeds much less than $\kc$, $\gamma$ is so close to 1 that proper and dilated times, and proper and contracted lengths, agree to more digits than anyone measures. This is why classical physics works for everyday motion, even though the effects are always present.

concepts.name: Length contraction
concepts.statement: Length contraction is the shortening of the measured length of an object moving relative to the observer's frame, along the direction of motion.

concepts.name: Classical velocity addition
concepts.statement: When $v \ll c$, velocities in one dimension add like ordinary numbers, with signs for direction: $u = v + u'$, where $v$ is the velocity between two observers and $u$ and $u'$ are the velocities of an object relative to each.

concepts.name: Relativistic velocity addition
concepts.statement: Velocities at relativistic speeds add by $u = (v + u')/(1 + vu'/c^2)$. The denominator is nearly 1 at low speeds, so the rule agrees with classical addition there; when either velocity is $\kc$ the result is exactly $\kc$, and velocities less than $\kc$ never add to more than $\kc$.

concepts.name: Adding relativistic velocities
concepts.statement: To add velocities relativistically, set up the two frames, choose the signs for direction, and apply the formula either way round, solving it for $u'$ or for the relative velocity $v$ where that is the unknown.

concepts.name: Relativistic Doppler shift of wavelength
concepts.statement: The relativistic Doppler effect is a change in the wavelength of radiation from a source moving relative to the observer. The wavelength is longer, a red shift, when the source moves away, and shorter, a blue shift, when it moves toward the observer, $\lambda_{\text{obs}} = \lambda_{\text{s}}\sqrt{(1 + u/c)/(1 - u/c)}$.

concepts.name: Relativistic Doppler shift of frequency
concepts.statement: Since every electromagnetic wave satisfies $c = f\lambda$, a longer wavelength means a lower frequency, and the frequency form of the relativistic Doppler shift has its signs the other way round, $f_{\text{obs}} = f_{\text{s}}\sqrt{(1 - u/c)/(1 + u/c)}$.

concepts.name: Relativistic momentum
concepts.statement: Relativistic momentum is $p = \gamma m u$, where $m$ is the rest mass of the object and $u$ its velocity relative to an observer. At low velocities it is the classical $mu$; near the speed of light it grows without limit.

concepts.name: Rest mass
concepts.statement: The rest mass of an object is its mass as measured by an observer at rest relative to it. Since the mass of a moving object can be found only through processes that involve momentum, the rest mass is the only meaningful mass, and $m$ means the rest mass.

concepts.name: Conservation of relativistic momentum
concepts.statement: Whenever the net external force on a system is zero, its total relativistic momentum is conserved, in every inertial frame.

concepts.name: Total energy
concepts.statement: The total energy of an object is defined as $E = \gamma mc^2$, the definition that makes energy conserved in every inertial frame. At rest, when $\gamma = 1$, the total energy is not zero.

concepts.name: Rest energy
concepts.statement: An object at rest has the rest energy $E_0 = mc^2$. Since $c^2$ is a very large number, the rest energy of even a gram of matter is enormous.

concepts.name: Mass-energy equivalence
concepts.statement: Mass is a form of energy rather than something separate. Energy stored in a charged battery or a compressed spring increases its rest mass, and in nuclear processes a measurable amount of mass is destroyed and its energy released.

concepts.name: Finding a mass change from an energy
concepts.statement: A change in rest mass follows from an energy stored or released by $\Delta m = \Delta E/c^2$, and the ratio $\Delta m/m$ shows whether the change could ever be noticed.

concepts.name: Relativistic kinetic energy
concepts.statement: The net work on an object that starts from rest raises its energy from $mc^2$ to $\gamma mc^2$, and the difference is its relativistic kinetic energy, $\text{KE}_{\text{rel}} = (\gamma - 1)mc^2$. Near the speed of light it is far larger than the classical value.

concepts.name: Classical limit of relativistic kinetic energy
concepts.statement: At low velocities the binomial expansion gives $\gamma \approx 1 + \frac{1}{2}v^2/c^2$, and substituting it turns $(\gamma - 1)mc^2$ into the classical kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$.

concepts.name: Speed of light as a limit
concepts.statement: As $v$ approaches $c$, $\gamma$ and with it the kinetic energy grow without limit, so an infinite amount of work would be needed to bring a mass to the speed of light. However much energy is put in, the velocity of an object with mass can only approach $c$.

concepts.name: Relativistic energy and momentum
concepts.statement: Relativistic energy and momentum are related by $E^2 = (pc)^2 + (mc^2)^2$. At rest this gives the rest energy, and at very high velocities the rest energy becomes negligible, so that $E \approx pc$.

concepts.name: Massless particles
concepts.statement: Setting $m = 0$ in the energy-momentum relation leaves $E = pc$, so a particle with no mass can still have momentum, and it must travel at the speed of light and only at that speed. Photons are such particles.

concepts.name: Ray
concepts.statement: A ray is a straight line that originates at some point. Light travels in straight lines, and modeling it as a bundle of rays lets us describe mirrors, lenses and images with nothing more than geometry and simple trigonometry.

concepts.name: Three paths of light
concepts.statement: Light can travel from a source to another location in three ways: directly through empty space, through a medium such as air or glass, or after reflecting from something. Every situation in geometric optics is one of these three or a combination of them.

concepts.name: Ray approximation
concepts.statement: Light behaves like a ray when it interacts with objects several times as large as its wavelength. The wavelength of visible light is less than a micron, so this covers nearly everything we can see with unaided eyes. For smaller objects the wave characteristics of light dominate.

concepts.name: Geometric optics
concepts.statement: Geometric optics is the part of optics in which the ray aspect of light dominates, so that geometry and simple trigonometry describe light fully. Two laws govern it: the law of reflection, for light that bounces off matter, and the law of refraction, for light that passes through it.

concepts.name: Law of reflection
concepts.statement: The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence. Both angles are measured from the perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray strikes it, not from the surface itself.

concepts.name: Specular and diffuse reflection
concepts.statement: The law of reflection holds at every point of every surface, and yet a mirror and a sheet of paper look nothing alike. The difference is the surface. A mirror is smooth compared with the wavelength of light and sends parallel rays away in one direction, while a rough surface meets each ray at a different angle and scatters them in many directions. That is why you see a mirror only from a particular angle and a piece of paper from any angle at all, and it is why most of the world around us is visible.

concepts.name: Image distance in a flat mirror
concepts.statement: When we look in a mirror, the image appears to be behind it, and the law of reflection says exactly where. The rays that reach the eye come from a direction fixed by the law, and extending them back places the image the same distance behind the mirror as the object stands in front of it. It is the first image in the book and the first case of light that only appears to come from a place, and 25.6 and 25.7 build on it.

concepts.name: Mirror
concepts.statement: A mirror is a smooth surface that reflects light at specific angles, forming an image of the person or object in front of it.

concepts.name: Angle of incidence
concepts.statement: The angle of incidence is the angle between an incoming ray and the perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray strikes it.

concepts.name: Angle of reflection
concepts.statement: The angle of reflection is the angle between a reflected ray and the perpendicular to the surface at the point where the ray strikes it.

concepts.name: Refraction
concepts.statement: Refraction is the changing of a light ray's direction when it passes through variations in matter. It makes a fish appear to be in two places at once, makes a pool look shallower than it is, and makes a lens work.

concepts.name: Speed of light in a vacuum
concepts.statement: The speed of light in a vacuum, $c = 2.99792458 \times 10^{8}$ m/s, is fixed by definition and is one of the basic physical quantities. It does not depend on the motion of the source or the observer, and light never travels faster than this.

concepts.name: Index of refraction
concepts.statement: The index of refraction of a material is the speed of light in a vacuum divided by its speed in the material, so a large index means a slow medium. Because light is never faster in matter than in a vacuum, the index is always one or greater, and the indices of gases are so close to one that we take them to be one.

concepts.name: Finding the speed of light in a material
concepts.statement: Rearranging $n = c/v$ into $v = c/n$ gives the speed of light in a material from its index of refraction, which tells how much slower light is in water or glass than in air.

concepts.name: Law of refraction
concepts.statement: The law of refraction, or Snell's law, ties the two angles a ray makes with the perpendicular to the indices of refraction of the two media, $n_1 \sin\theta_1 = n_2 \sin\theta_2$, so that any three of the four quantities give the fourth.

concepts.name: Bending toward or away from the perpendicular
concepts.statement: Light entering a slower medium bends toward the perpendicular, and light entering a faster medium bends away from it. The larger the change in speed, the larger the change in direction.

concepts.name: Applying Snell’s law
concepts.statement: Given both angles, Snell's law yields the index of refraction of an unknown medium, which is how a measurement identifies a substance. Given the two indices and the incident angle, it yields the refracted angle.

concepts.name: Angle of refraction
concepts.statement: The angle of refraction is the angle between a refracted ray and the perpendicular to the surface, in the medium the ray crosses into.

concepts.name: Critical angle
concepts.statement: The critical angle is the incident angle that produces an angle of refraction of 90°. It exists only for light going from a medium of larger index into one of smaller index, where the ray bends away from the perpendicular.

concepts.name: Critical angle from the indices
concepts.statement: Putting a refracted angle of 90° into Snell's law leaves $n_1 \sin\theta_1 = n_2$, so the critical angle is $\theta_{\text{c}} = \sin^{-1}(n_2/n_1)$, and it exists only when $n_1$ is larger than $n_2$. The critical angle is a property of a pair of materials, not of one.

concepts.name: Total internal reflection
concepts.statement: Beyond the critical angle no light crosses the boundary: every ray is reflected back into the first medium. Total internal reflection is a perfect mirror, better than any silvered surface, which absorbs part of the light that falls on it.

concepts.name: Finding a critical angle
concepts.statement: To find a critical angle, take the medium the light travels in as medium 1, look up or measure the two indices, and take the inverse sine of $n_2/n_1$. Run backward, the same step turns a measured critical angle into the index of an unknown substance.

concepts.name: Fiber optics
concepts.statement: Fiber optics is the transmission of light down fibers of plastic or glass by total internal reflection. Light entering a thin fiber strikes its inside surface at angles greater than the critical angle and follows the fiber even around corners, and a cladding of lower index keeps the light in one fiber from crossing into its neighbor.

concepts.name: Corner reflector
concepts.statement: A corner reflector is two mutually perpendicular reflecting surfaces, which return light exactly parallel to the direction from which it came, whatever the angle of incidence. Made of glass rather than silvered mirrors, it is perfectly efficient, because the reflections are total.

concepts.name: Sparkle of a diamond
concepts.statement: Diamond's index of refraction is so large that its critical angle with air is only 24.4°, so light that enters it has trouble getting out again. The facets are cut so that the light can leave in only a few directions, and it comes out concentrated at those few places.

concepts.name: Zircon
concepts.statement: Zircon is a natural gemstone with a large index of refraction, about 1.9, which makes it sparkle in the way a diamond does.

concepts.name: Dispersion
concepts.statement: Dispersion is the spreading of white light into its full spectrum of wavelengths. More generally, it occurs whenever a process changes the direction of light in a way that depends on wavelength, and it can happen to any kind of wave.

concepts.name: Color and wavelength
concepts.statement: We see each pure wavelength of visible light as one of about six colors, from red at the long end to violet at the short, and white light is a nearly uniform mixture of all of them. A spreading by wavelength is therefore a spreading into colors.

concepts.name: Index of refraction and wavelength
concepts.statement: For a given medium the index of refraction depends on wavelength, growing slowly as the wavelength falls, so violet light meets a larger index than red light in the same glass and is bent more by refraction.

concepts.name: Rainbow formation
concepts.statement: A rainbow is made when sunlight refracts as it enters a water drop, reflects from the back of the drop and refracts again as it leaves. Because the index depends on wavelength, the colors leave at slightly different angles, and only drops at the one correct angle from the line between the observer and the sun send a given color to the eye, so the colors form an arc.

concepts.name: Rainbow
concepts.statement: A rainbow is the dispersion of sunlight into a continuous distribution of colors according to wavelength, produced by the refraction and reflection of sunlight by water droplets in the sky.

concepts.name: Converging and diverging lenses
concepts.statement: A converging lens is a convex lens, thicker in the middle, which brings rays that enter it parallel to its axis together at a single point on the opposite side. A diverging lens is a concave lens, thicker at the edges, which bends such rays away from its axis.

concepts.name: Focal point and focal length
concepts.statement: The focal point of a converging lens or mirror is the point at which rays arriving parallel to the axis cross; for a diverging lens or mirror it is the point from which they appear to originate. The focal length is the distance from the center of the lens or mirror to its focal point, positive for a converging lens and negative for a diverging one.

concepts.name: Power of a lens
concepts.statement: The power of a lens is the inverse of its focal length, $P = 1/f$, measured in diopters when the focal length is in meters. A short focal length is a powerful lens that bends light strongly. This power has nothing to do with the power in watts of Chapter 7.

concepts.name: Tracing rays through a thin lens
concepts.statement: Ray tracing finds an image with nothing but a straight edge. A ray arriving parallel to the axis leaves through the focal point, a ray through the center goes straight on, and a ray through the near focal point leaves parallel to the axis. Two rays locate an image, and a third is a check.

concepts.name: Real and virtual images
concepts.statement: A real image is one that can be projected: the rays from a point on the object actually cross, so a screen, a piece of film or a retina can catch it. A virtual image cannot be projected: the rays only appear to come from a common point, and a screen put there catches nothing.

concepts.name: Thin lens equation
concepts.statement: The thin lens equation relates the object distance, the image distance and the focal length, so that any one of the three follows from the other two. A negative image distance means the image is virtual and on the same side as the object.

concepts.name: Magnification
concepts.statement: The magnification is the ratio of image height to object height, and it equals minus the ratio of image distance to object distance. A negative magnification means the image is inverted, and a magnitude greater or less than one says whether it is enlarged or reduced.

concepts.name: Three cases of thin lens images
concepts.statement: A converging lens with the object farther away than the focal length makes a real, inverted image. The same lens with the object closer makes an enlarged, upright, virtual image, which is what a magnifier does. A diverging lens always makes a reduced, upright, virtual image, whatever the object distance.

concepts.name: Solving a lens problem
concepts.statement: Identify the case from the sign of the focal length and the object distance. Solve the thin lens equation for the unknown distance, remembering to invert $1/d_{\text{i}}$ at the end, and then take the magnification from the two distances. Finally, check the answer against the case: a case 2 image must come out virtual, upright and enlarged, and an answer that does not is a mistake in the arithmetic rather than a discovery.

concepts.name: Object distance
concepts.statement: The object distance is the distance of an object from the center of a lens or mirror.

concepts.name: Image distance
concepts.statement: The image distance is the distance of an image from the center of a lens or mirror. It is positive for a real image and negative for a virtual one.

concepts.name: Converging lens
concepts.statement: A converging lens is a convex lens in which light rays that enter it parallel to its axis converge at a single point on the opposite side.

concepts.name: Diverging lens
concepts.statement: A diverging lens is a concave lens in which light rays that enter it parallel to its axis bend away, or diverge, from its axis.

concepts.name: Focal point
concepts.statement: For a converging lens or mirror, the focal point is the point at which converging light rays cross; for a diverging lens or mirror, it is the point from which diverging light rays appear to originate.

concepts.name: Focal length
concepts.statement: The focal length is the distance from the center of a lens or curved mirror to its focal point. It is positive for a converging lens or mirror and negative for a diverging one.

concepts.name: Real image
concepts.statement: A real image is an image that can be projected: the rays from a point on the object actually cross there, so a screen can catch it.

concepts.name: Virtual image
concepts.statement: A virtual image is an image that cannot be projected: the rays from a point on the object only appear to come from it.

concepts.name: Image in a flat mirror
concepts.statement: The image in a flat mirror is virtual, upright and the same size as the object, and it lies as far behind the mirror as the object stands in front of it. In the language of the thin lens equations, $d_{\text{i}} = -d_{\text{o}}$, which gives a magnification of exactly one and a mirror of infinite focal length.

concepts.name: Focal length of a spherical mirror
concepts.statement: A spherical mirror that is small compared with its radius of curvature brings parallel rays to a focus halfway between its surface and its center of curvature, so its focal length is half the radius, $f = R/2$. The power $P = 1/f$ is defined for a mirror exactly as for a lens.

concepts.name: Converging and diverging mirrors
concepts.statement: A converging mirror is a concave mirror, which brings rays striking it parallel to its axis together in front of itself and has a positive focal length. A diverging mirror is a convex mirror, which spreads such rays so that they appear to come from a point behind it and has a negative focal length.

concepts.name: Tracing rays at a mirror
concepts.statement: The rules for tracing rays at a mirror are the rules for lenses with the light sent back the way it came. A ray arriving parallel to the axis leaves through the focal point, or appears to come from it. A ray striking the center leaves at the same angle to the axis. A ray through the focal point leaves parallel to the axis.

concepts.name: Three cases of mirror images
concepts.statement: A concave mirror with the object farther away than the focal length makes a real, inverted image on the same side as the object. The same mirror with the object closer makes an enlarged, upright, virtual image behind it, which is what a makeup mirror does. A convex mirror always makes a reduced, upright, virtual image, which is what a security mirror does.

concepts.name: Solving a mirror problem
concepts.statement: For a mirror small compared with its radius of curvature, the thin lens equation and the magnification hold unchanged, with the focal length equal to half the radius of curvature and signed by the kind of mirror. Find the focal length, solve for the unknown distance, take the magnification, and check the answer against the case.

concepts.name: Mirror and lens analogy
concepts.statement: Mirrors form exactly the same three types of image as lenses do, with the same signs and the same conditions: a concave mirror acts like a convex lens, and a convex mirror like a concave lens.

concepts.name: Radius of curvature of a mirror
concepts.statement: The radius of curvature of a spherical mirror is the radius of the sphere of which the mirror is a part, the distance from the mirror's surface to its center of curvature.

concepts.name: Converging mirror
concepts.statement: A converging mirror is a concave mirror in which light rays that strike it parallel to its axis converge at one or more points along the axis.

concepts.name: Diverging mirror
concepts.statement: A diverging mirror is a convex mirror in which light rays that strike it parallel to its axis bend away, or diverge, from its axis.

concepts.name: Radiopharmaceutical
concepts.statement: A radiopharmaceutical is a compound tagged with a radioactive nuclide and chosen because the body sends it to the organ under study. Because $\gamma$ rays pass easily out of the body and a nucleus radiates the same whatever compound it sits in, detectors outside the body can see where the compound has gone.

concepts.name: Technetium-99m
concepts.statement: One nuclide carries perhaps 80 percent of all nuclear medicine, and the reasons are the chapter's physics in miniature: a single clean $\gamma$ energy, a short half-life that limits the dose, and a parent that decays into it on site.

concepts.name: Anger camera
concepts.statement: The Anger camera images a radiopharmaceutical with a lead collimator that passes only $\gamma$ rays traveling along its holes, a scintillator that turns each $\gamma$ ray into light, and photomultipliers that turn the light into a signal. The image it forms is flat and carries no depth.

concepts.name: SPECT
concepts.statement: Single-photon-emission computed tomography images a $\gamma$-emitting radiopharmaceutical. It surrounds the patient with detectors and combines their images by computer into a three-dimensional picture, as x-ray CT does for shadows. It gains depth at the cost of resolution.

concepts.name: PET
concepts.statement: PET is the cleanest use of conservation laws in medicine: an annihilating positron and electron at rest must send two equal 0.511-MeV $\gamma$ rays in opposite directions, so two detectors firing together name the line the source lies on.

concepts.name: Finding a mass from activity
concepts.statement: The mass of a radioactive sample follows from its activity and half-life: the activity and half-life give the number of nuclei, and Avogadro's number and the molar mass turn that number into a mass. Medical activities of a few millicuries correspond to astonishingly small masses.

concepts.name: Tagged compound
concepts.statement: A compound is tagged when a radioactive nuclide is attached to it, so that the nuclide's radiation shows where the compound goes.

concepts.name: Radiation damage to DNA
concepts.statement: Every biological effect of radiation, from cancer to its cure, follows from this one statement. It explains why rapidly reproducing cells, including cancer cells, are the most sensitive.

concepts.name: Radiation dose
concepts.statement: The absorbed dose is the ionizing energy deposited per kilogram of the tissue affected. It is measured in rad, where $1\;\text{rad} = 0.01\;\text{J/kg}$, or in gray, where $1\;\text{Gy} = 1\;\text{J/kg} = 100\;\text{rad}$.

concepts.name: Relative biological effectiveness
concepts.statement: The relative biological effectiveness (RBE), or quality factor, of a type of radiation is the factor by which its biological effect per unit of absorbed dose exceeds that of x rays. Short-range radiation such as $\alpha$ particles concentrates its damage, which is harder to repair, and so has a large RBE.

concepts.name: Dose equivalent
concepts.statement: The dose equivalent is the absorbed dose multiplied by the RBE, a number proportional to the biological effect: $\text{rem} = \text{rad}\times\text{RBE}$ and $\text{Sv} = \text{Gy}\times\text{RBE}$. Dose limits and risks are stated in this quantity.

concepts.name: Calculating a dose
concepts.statement: The dose from a source is found by following its decays into joules per kilogram: the activity and time give the number of decays, the energy per decay gives the energy deposited, the mass of tissue gives the dose in grays, and the RBE gives the dose in sieverts. Activity is not to be confused with dose along the way.

concepts.name: Immediate effects of a dose
concepts.statement: A single whole-body dose below about 0.1 Sv has no observable immediate effect, a dose near 1 Sv causes radiation sickness, and a dose near 5 Sv is fatal to about half of those who receive it. Blood counts fall first because blood cells reproduce fastest.

concepts.name: Linear hypothesis
concepts.statement: The linear hypothesis assumes that the risk of a radiation-induced cancer is proportional to the dose, even at doses too low for any effect to be observed. Scaling down from high doses in this way gives about $10/10^{6}\;\text{rem}\cdot\text{y}$ for the risk of cancer.

concepts.name: Background radiation
concepts.statement: Everyone receives background radiation, about 3 mSv a year on average, from cosmic rays, from rocks and soil, from the body's own nuclides and, above all, from radon. Its size varies from place to place and is the natural yardstick for every other dose.

concepts.name: Radiation protection
concepts.statement: A dose is limited in only three ways: by keeping the time of exposure short, by increasing the distance from the source and by placing shielding between the source and the body.

concepts.name: Rad
concepts.statement: The rad, short for radiation absorbed dose, is the dose that deposits 0.01 J of ionizing energy in each kilogram of tissue.

concepts.name: Gray
concepts.statement: The gray is the SI unit of absorbed dose, the dose that deposits 1 J of ionizing energy in each kilogram of tissue; one gray is 100 rad.

concepts.name: Rem
concepts.statement: The rem, short for roentgen equivalent man, is the unit of dose equivalent that goes with the rad: a dose in rad times the RBE of the radiation gives the dose equivalent in rem.

concepts.name: Sievert
concepts.statement: The sievert is the SI unit of dose equivalent: a dose in grays times the RBE of the radiation gives the dose equivalent in sieverts, and one sievert is 100 rem.

concepts.name: Low dose
concepts.statement: A low dose is a dose of less than about 0.1 Sv (10 rem), below which no immediate effect can be observed.

concepts.name: Moderate dose
concepts.statement: A moderate dose is a dose from about 0.1 Sv to 1 Sv (10 to 100 rem), which can cause measurable changes in the blood and, near the top of the range, radiation sickness.

concepts.name: High dose
concepts.statement: A high dose is a dose greater than about 1 Sv (100 rem), which causes radiation sickness and, at several sieverts, can be fatal.

concepts.name: Hormesis
concepts.statement: Hormesis is the proposal that a very low dose of radiation may be beneficial, stimulating the body's repair mechanisms; the evidence for it is not conclusive.

concepts.name: Shielding
concepts.statement: Shielding is a layer of material placed between a radiation source and the body to absorb the radiation and so reduce the dose.

concepts.name: Therapeutic ratio
concepts.statement: Radiotherapy works because cancer cells, reproducing rapidly, are more sensitive to radiation than normal cells. Every technique aims to kill as many abnormal cells as possible for each normal cell killed.

concepts.name: Crossfire beams
concepts.statement: A single beam would give healthy tissue on its path the same dose as the tumor. Rotating the source about a point in the tumor keeps the dose high at the crossing point and spreads it thin everywhere else.

concepts.name: Therapeutic doses
concepts.statement: Doses of tens of sieverts would kill if given to the whole body at once. Localization and fractionation make them survivable, and the tolerable dose depends on the surrounding tissue.

concepts.name: Radiotherapy
concepts.statement: Radiotherapy is the use of ionizing radiation to treat disease, above all to destroy cancer cells.

concepts.name: Food irradiation
concepts.statement: Food irradiation is the treatment of food with ionizing radiation. It reduces pest infestation, delays spoilage and prevents illness caused by microorganisms, and because insects and bacteria tolerate far more radiation than people, it takes doses of thousands of grays.

concepts.name: No residual radioactivity in irradiated food
